title: Release guard and registry credentials sit only in workflow code that any branch or tag author supplies
description: release.yml's guard job (release.yml:24-58) is meant to stop a hand-pushed tag from publishing unless the tagged commit is on main and ci.yml passed for it (comment at release.yml:15-23, backlog 1.32). On a `push` event, GitHub runs the workflow file from the pushed commit (GITHUB_SHA). The guard therefore lives in the same file the tag author chooses, and the publish job's only link to it is `needs: guard` (release.yml:61). The release job has no `environment:` key, and no workflow in .github/workflows declares one. DOCKERHUB_USERNAME/DOCKERHUB_TOKEN (release.yml:118-119) and HARBOR_USERNAME/HARBOR_PASSWORD (release.yml:125-126) are therefore repository or organization secrets. GitHub gives those to any workflow run on any branch or tag of the repository that is not a fork pull request. A principal who can push a v* tag, or any branch carrying a workflow that names these secrets, can drop or edit the guard and push noixdev/pulsix-manager and noixdev/pulsix-worker images to Docker Hub and Harbor, including `latest`. Branch protection on main does not stop that principal. The compose stack defaults to `latest` (deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml:40, 123, 155), so an installation that keeps the default would pull such an image into the manager, which holds the master key and DB URL, and into the worker, which holds its mTLS identity and runs plays with job credentials. tag.yml (workflow_dispatch only, tag.yml:37; `contents: write`, tag.yml:46; `secrets: inherit`, tag.yml:61) is the same exposure through another route. A write user can dispatch it from a branch whose tag.yml they edited, and the 7.16 SHA pin applies only to the main copy. Any branch workflow could also reference the secrets directly, so this adds no new principal. A secondary weakness weakens the guard even when it runs from a genuine main release.yml. Its CI query (release.yml:52-54) takes the newest ci.yml run for the SHA with no event or branch filter. ci.yml triggers on pull_request (ci.yml:2), and a pull_request run uses the workflow file from the PR merge ref but reports the PR head as head_sha. A writer who controls a PR's base branch can therefore produce a green ci.yml run for an existing main commit that originally failed CI. This lets a tag-capable writer publish reviewed main code that failed CI. It does not let them publish arbitrary code. Whether the exposure is real depends on hosted facts: who holds write or tag rights without release authority, where the secrets are scoped, and whether Actions is enabled. Local git history shows a single author (946 commits), and backlog 1.44 and 7.17 say workflows are prepared but not enabled while the repo is private. Backlog 7.16 already lists 'registry secrets belong in a protected release environment' as open.
claimed_root_cause: Release authorization is enforced only in workflow code that the triggering ref supplies: the guard job in release.yml, plus tag.yml when it is dispatched from a branch. The registry push credentials are not bound to a protected GitHub environment with tag-only deployment rules or required reviewers. Nothing outside the attacker-editable workflow file separates a release-authorized principal from any principal who can push a ref. The guard's CI query also accepts a ci.yml run of any event type, so a pull_request run whose workflow came from an attacker-controlled base branch counts as a pass.

trace.description: A v* tag push starts the workflow. For push events GitHub runs the workflow definition stored at the pushed commit (GITHUB_SHA), so the tag author chooses which release.yml runs, including one without the guard job.

The on-main check (lines 34-42) and the CI-green check (lines 44-58) live in the same tag-supplied file. The CI query at lines 52-54 is `workflows/ci.yml/runs?head_sha=$SHA&per_page=1`, with no event=push or branch=main filter, so it takes the newest ci.yml run of any event for that SHA.

The publish job's only dependency on the guard is `needs: guard` in the same file. The job has no `environment:` key, so GitHub evaluates no deployment protection rule (tag pattern, reviewers) before giving it secrets.

workflow_dispatch runs the tag.yml of whatever branch the dispatcher selects, with `contents: write` and `secrets: inherit`. A write user who edits tag.yml on a branch bypasses the commit pin at line 60, which protects only the main copy. This adds no new principal, because a branch workflow can name the secrets directly.

trace.scope: jobs.release: Docker Hub/Harbor login (lines 115-126) and build-push (lines 128-156)
trace.description: secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN (line 119) and secrets.HARBOR_PASSWORD (line 126) are used with no environment. build-push-action then pushes the vX.Y.Z and `latest` tags of noixdev/pulsix-manager and noixdev/pulsix-worker to Docker Hub and harbor.cloud.noidee.dev.

evidence.description: The comment states the intended invariant: a tag is not evidence, a hand-pushed tag must not be trusted, and the thing that publishes does the checking.
The comment's safety argument covers fork PRs only. It assumes anyone with write access who creates a tag is fine, which is the assumption the guard was added to drop.
Harbor credentials (lines 125-126), like Docker Hub's (lines 118-119), are referenced in a job with no `environment:`. No workflow under .github/workflows declares any environment.
The guard's CI query is scoped to the workflow file and head_sha only, with no event or branch filter.
ci.yml also triggers on pull_request. That run's workflow definition comes from the PR merge ref, while its head_sha is the PR head, so it can satisfy the guard's query.
`secrets: inherit` remains, together with workflow_dispatch (line 37) and `contents: write` (line 46). The pin at line 60 binds only the copy of tag.yml that is dispatched.
The manager runs noixdev/pulsix-manager:${PULSIX_VERSION:-latest}. worker-enroll (line 123) and worker (line 155) use the same default, so a pushed `latest` reaches installations that keep it.
Backlog 7.16 lists 'the registry secrets belong in a protected release environment (1.38)' as still open outside this repo. That confirms they are not environment-bound today.
Backlog 1.44 says the workflows are prepared but not enabled while the repo is private, so today the path may not run at all.

blockers: Hosted fact: the scope of DOCKERHUB_USERNAME, DOCKERHUB_TOKEN, HARBOR_USERNAME and HARBOR_PASSWORD (repository or organization secret, and for an organization secret its repository access list). Source shows only that they are not environment secrets.

Hosted fact: whether any principal can push a branch or a v* tag, or dispatch workflows, without being authorized to cut releases. This needs the collaborator, team and app/bot list with write access, branch protection on main, and any tag ruleset on refs/tags/v*. Local history has a single author. If every writer is a release manager, the bypass is same-principal and not a vulnerability.

Hosted fact: whether GitHub Actions is enabled for NoiXdev/pulsix (backlog 1.44/7.17 say it is not while the repo is private), and whether the Docker Hub/Harbor images are published and consumed by any installation yet.
No safe local check: proving it needs a real GitHub Actions run, and this audit may not contact GitHub or publish anything.

validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed only. Push no tag and no image. (1) In NoiXdev/pulsix Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions, and in the NoiXdev organization equivalent, confirm whether the four registry secrets are repository or organization secrets and not environment secrets. For organization secrets, note which repositories can use them. (2) In Settings > Collaborators and teams, plus installed GitHub Apps, list every principal with write or maintain access. In Settings > Rules / Branches, check main's protection and whether a ruleset restricts creating refs/tags/v* to release managers. (3) Confirm whether Actions is enabled for the repository. The finding holds if the secrets are repository- or organization-scoped and any write principal (or an app with contents:write) is not meant to release. Fix: create a `release` environment whose deployment branch/tag rule allows only v* tags (backed by a tag ruleset limiting who creates them), optionally with a required reviewer. Move the four registry secrets into it and add `environment: release` to jobs.release. Scope the guard's CI query to `&event=push&branch=main`. Replace tag.yml's `secrets: inherit` with the single declared secret once the shared workflow declares it (backlog 7.16 follow-up).
validation_plan.local: Use only a throwaway personal fixture repository, never NoiXdev/pulsix, with a dummy repository secret REG_TOKEN=marker and no registry login. (a) On main, commit a release.yml with a guard job (fails unless the commit is on main) and a release job that prints sha256(REG_TOKEN). On a side branch, commit a copy with the guard removed and push tag v0.0.0-test at that side commit. Observe that the guardless definition runs and the release job reads the secret. (b) Move REG_TOKEN into an environment `release` restricted to protected v* tags, with a tag ruleset limiting creation, and add `environment: release`. Repeat and observe that the secret is withheld or the job waits for approval. (c) For the CI query: open a PR whose head is an existing commit X and whose base branch carries a ci.yml that always succeeds. Then query actions/workflows/ci.yml/runs?head_sha=X&per_page=1 and observe whether the newest run is the pull_request run with conclusion success.

title: Any enrolled agent can trigger unlimited organization-wide resolves against the shared database by sending heartbeats in a loop
description: Every Heartbeat message on an AgentStream runs a full, uncached checks.ResolveHost for the agent's organization before the version is compared. That means a Touch UPDATE, a SELECT * of every host row in the organization (MonitoredHosts -> ListAllHosts, used only to filter monitored ids), ListDefinitions, the monitoring-group list, and one selector query per monitoring group (QueryHosts, a DISTINCT ON CTE over the organization's host_tags joined to its hosts). The server sets no limit on how often one agent identity may send heartbeats. There is no per-stream or per-serial message rate limit, no bundle cache (backlog 3.19 is still 'idea'), and no cap on how many streams one serial may hold open: StreamRegistry.track adds every stream to byHost, and grpc.NewServer sets no MaxConcurrentStreams or tap handle. The intended 30 s cadence lives only in the honest agent's own ticker. A small protobuf message therefore costs 4+G statements (Touch plus 3+G resolve reads). Each read grows with the organization's host and tag count, and H, T and G are writable by operator+ without quota. All of these statements run on the single pgx pool and manager process that every tenant shares. A local reproduction with the real checks.Service sent 600 heartbeats, 200 on each of 3 concurrently open streams of one enrolled agent, in an organization with 10 groups. Every heartbeat was acknowledged within about 17 ms in total, with no throttling, and they caused 7800 resolve-time store or port calls (13 per heartbeat). The owner's own backlog 3.19 measurement of 28.3 ms per resolve at 1000 hosts and 5 groups puts one looping stream at roughly one saturated core. A handful of streams can therefore keep connections in the shared pool busy continuously.
root_cause: processHeartbeat (internal/agentapi/stream.go:166-173) treats every received Heartbeat as a reason to run an uncached, organization-wide ResolveHost, before and regardless of the version comparison. Nothing on the server bounds how often one agent identity can trigger it: there is no rate limit or minimum interval in receiveMessages or processHeartbeat, no cache in checks.Service.loadResolveBundle, no per-serial stream cap in StreamRegistry.track, and no stream or tap limit on the gRPC server.
intended_behavior: The server should bound the work one agent identity can cause on the shared pool, rather than relying on the agent to behave. Resolves should be rate-limited or coalesced per stream or serial and per organization, for example a minimum interval between resolves per stream answered from the last result, plus a short-TTL per-organization bundle cache. The number of concurrent AgentStreams per agent serial should also be capped.

trace.description: The mTLS-authenticated agent's AgentStream receive loop reads each AgentMessage, with no rate, interval or count check. It then hands the message to s.process at line 102.
A Heartbeat body is routed to processHeartbeat (line 138).
After the Touch UPDATE (line 167), ResolveHost runs unconditionally on every heartbeat, before the version comparison at line 195.
MonitoredHosts reads every host of the organization, through hosts.ListAllHosts (SELECT * FROM hosts WHERE org_id=$1). It then calls loadResolveBundle.
After ListDefinitions (line 89) and List groups (line 93), the loop issues one MatchingHosts selector query per monitoring group. Nothing is cached.
Per group, a DISTINCT ON CTE runs over the organization's host_tags plus the matched host rows. It executes on the shared pool.

evidence.description: grpc.NewServer sets only creds, message-size limits, auth interceptors and keepalive MaxConnectionAge. It has no MaxConcurrentStreams, InTapHandle or per-identity limiter for agent streams.
StreamRegistry.track adds every new stream of a host to byHost[hostID] with no cap. The local run kept 3 streams of one serial tracked at once.
MonitoredHosts loads every host of the organization in full, through ListAllHosts, only to filter the monitored ids.
ListAllHosts is an unpaginated SELECT * over the organization's hosts, including the facts and vars JSON columns.
A single pgxpool serves all tenants. Code sets no pool size and no statement timeout, so the pgx defaults apply unless the DSN sets them.
processHeartbeat's own comment acknowledges the organization-wide resolve on every heartbeat (backlog 3.19).

Backlog 3.19 ('idea') records the owner's measurement of 28.3 ms per resolve at 1000 hosts and 5 groups, framed as fleet-scale cost. It does not address an agent that heartbeats faster than its 30 s ticker.
The existing test asserts one ResolveHost per heartbeat, even for heartbeats that report the converged version.

conditions.description: The attacker holds a valid, unrevoked agent certificate for one host. That means root on any monitored host of the organization, which is a lower-trust principal with no REST access, or any user who can enroll an agent: operator+ in an organization, and any MFA-complete user can create their own organization.
The attacker must be able to reach the manager's gRPC listener (8444), which agents need anyway. The default compose file does not publish it on the host, but any deployment with remote agents does.
The per-heartbeat cost grows with the organization's host, tag and monitoring-group counts. The same tenant can raise all three without quota.
How far the load spreads to other tenants depends on the deployment's pool size (the pgx default unless the DSN sets one) and on any DSN-level statement_timeout. Code sets neither.

execution.attacker_perspective: One enrolled agent identity sends Heartbeat messages back to back on several concurrently open AgentStreams, instead of one every 30 s.
payloads: AgentMessage{Heartbeat{version:"x", config_version:"anything"}}, sent 200 times on each of 3 concurrently open AgentStreams of one agent, in an organization with 10 monitoring groups
instructions: Copied the repository to scratch and added internal/agentapi/zz_v13_heartbeat_test.go. It uses a real checks.Service (checks.NewService with WithHostRoster and WithMatcher) backed by counting fakes for Store.ListDefinitions, Store.List (10 groups), HostRoster.MonitoredHosts (returns the enrolled host) and HostMatcher.MatchingHosts.

Enrolled one agent through the package's own test harness (newHarnessPort, enrollAnAgent). Opened 3 AgentStreams, kept them all open, sent 200 heartbeats on each and read each acknowledgement. Then read the StreamRegistry's tracked-stream count for the host.

Ran it in the approved sandbox: go test -count=1 -v -run 'TestV13HeartbeatResolveFanOut|TestConvergenceUnrecognisedVersionPushesOnceThenConverges' ./internal/agentapi/ (no network, read-only source and module cache, 2 CPU / 2 GiB, 300 s limit).
execution.observed_result: concurrently tracked streams for this one host/serial: 3. streams=3 heartbeats_per_stream=200 acked=600 groups=10 elapsed=16.744667ms. downstream: MonitoredHosts=600 ListDefinitions=600 ListGroups=600 MatchingHosts=6000 total=7800 (3+G=13 per heartbeat). No heartbeat was throttled or refused. The repository's own TestConvergenceUnrecognisedVersionPushesOnceThenConverges also passed, asserting one resolve per heartbeat. The Touch UPDATE on each heartbeat ran against a fake store, so it is not counted in the 7800.

remediation.strategy: Bound resolve work per agent identity on the server. In processHeartbeat, if this stream resolved less than a minimum interval ago (for example 10 s), skip the resolve and answer from the last ResolvedSet. Put a short-TTL per-organization bundle cache in front of loadResolveBundle (backlog 3.19's named mitigation), so concurrent heartbeats of one organization share one load. Cap concurrent AgentStreams per agent serial in StreamRegistry.track: refuse, or close the oldest stream, beyond a small number such as 2. Optionally set grpc.MaxConcurrentStreams. Add a regression test showing that 100 heartbeats inside one interval cause at most one ResolveHost, and that a third stream for one serial is refused.

likelihood.reason: The attack needs one valid agent certificate. Root on any monitored host has one, and any user who can create an organization or holds operator+ can obtain one. The loop is trivial and no server-side control stops it.

impact.reason: Each tiny message costs 4+G organization-wide statements on the pool and manager process that all tenants share: 13 store or port calls per heartbeat locally, and about 28 ms of resolve work per heartbeat at 1000 hosts per the owner's measurement. Several looping streams can therefore degrade other tenants' API, ingest and alerting. The effect is not persistent. It needs sustained sending from an attributable serial, and stops when the streams stop or the certificate is revoked.

confidence.reason: Source and a sandboxed run with the real stream and checks.Service code establish both the missing server-side bound (per message and per serial stream count) and the 1:(3+G) resolve fan-out per heartbeat. The absolute database cost, and the point where the shared pool saturates, depend on the deployment's pool size, statement timeout and data volume. Those were not measured, because no Postgres runs in the sandbox.

title: The agent install command puts the enrollment token in the process arguments of the root installer, where any local user on the host can read it
description: When an admin creates an agent enrollment token (POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/agents/tokens), the manager returns an install command that the Add-agent dialog tells the operator to run as root on the host: `curl -fsSL <manager>/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- --token pxa1.<id>.<secret>.<pin> --manager <addr>`. The full token becomes a command-line argument of the sudo process and of the root `sh -s` installer. deploy/install.sh accepts the token only through argv (`--token`). Both processes stay alive for the whole install: two downloads from the manager, the checksum check, the file writes and `systemctl enable --now`. On Linux, /proc/<pid>/cmdline has mode 0444 unless /proc is mounted with hidepid, so any unprivileged local user or service account on that host can read the token, for example with ps or by polling /proc. The installer treats the token as a root-only secret. It writes the token under umask 077 into a 0600 /etc/pulsix/agent.env inside a 0700 directory, and its header says the token is written owner-only. The argv copy bypasses that boundary. The token works for anyone who presents it: the anonymous gRPC Enroll checks only the secret, expiry and remaining uses, so the first redeemer wins. A local reader who redeems the token gets an org-SAN agent mTLS identity. If the token is bound to a host, Register makes the reader the host's active agent and revokes any previous serial, and the genuine agent's single-use enrollment is refused. From then on the reader controls that host's facts, auto tags, check results and heartbeats. With an unbound or multi-use token (up to 100 uses and 7 days), the reader can enroll extra monitored hosts into the organization. sudo's default command logging probably keeps a longer-lived copy in the auth log or journal, but that was not checked locally. The worker docker-run snippet (internal/api/worker_snippets.go:29) passes its enrollment token on the command line too, as `-e PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN=...`.
root_cause: agentInstallCommand (internal/api/agent_handlers.go:349) formats the secret into the command line (`sudo sh -s -- --token %s`), and deploy/install.sh (lines 48-54) reads the token only from a positional argv value. No root-only channel such as a 0600 file, a /dev/tty prompt or stdin is offered, so the secret sits in world-readable process metadata for the whole install.
intended_behavior: On the target host, only root can read the enrollment token, as deploy/install.sh:21 documents. The token reaches the installer through a channel that other local users and system logs cannot read, such as a no-echo prompt on /dev/tty or a root-owned 0600 file, and never appears in process arguments.

trace.description: A local user with fewer privileges than root reads the token. The printed command runs `sudo sh -s -- --token <pxa1 token> ...`, and install.sh takes the token only from argv (`--token) PULSIX_TOKEN="$2"`), so the token is in the cmdline of the sudo and root sh processes. That file has mode 0444 (observed) and stays readable for the whole install, which runs until `systemctl enable --now` at line 140.

The reader sends the copied token with its own CSR and a name to the unauthenticated Enroll, which the enrolling host must already be able to reach. Line 153 parses the pxa1 token. The only per-request limit is 10 attempts per minute per IP.
The claim checks only the secret hash, used_at and expiry. Nothing ties the token to the presenter or to the host, so whoever redeems first consumes the use.

The manager signs the attacker's CSR (line 205) and registers it as the host's active agent. Register revokes the host's previous serial (internal/agents/service.go:422-431), and line 224 closes that serial's streams. The attacker now holds an org-SAN agent identity for the host.

evidence.description: cmd := fmt.Sprintf("curl -fsSL %s/install.sh | sudo sh -s -- --token %s --manager %s", base, token, addr)
The token-create route returns InstallCommand built from the freshly printed pxa1 token.
The dialog shows the command with a Copy button and says 'Run this on the host as root.'
The header says the token is written owner-only into /etc/pulsix/agent.env, so the intended boundary is root-only.
chmod 600 on agent.env, after chmod 700 /etc/pulsix and umask 077 (lines 116-118). Only the file copy is protected; the argv copy is not.
The binary and checksum downloads (lines 103-104) and systemctl at line 140 run while the token is still in argv, so the exposure window lasts the whole install.
Register records the new agent and revokes the host's previous serial, so a reader who redeems a host-bound token replaces the genuine agent.
Tokens may live up to 7 days (maxTokenMinutes) and admit up to 100 agents (MaxUses maximum, line 103). The dialog defaults to 1 use.
A multi-use token stays claimable until max_uses is reached, so one leaked copy can enroll several presenters.

conditions.description: The attacker has an unprivileged local account or service account (below root) on the Linux host where an operator runs the printed install command.
/proc is mounted without hidepid=1 or 2, which is the default on mainstream distributions. Hosts with hidepid or a per-user PID namespace are not exposed through /proc.

With the default single-use token, the reader must read the token while the installer runs and redeem it before the agent enrolls on first start, a window that covers the binary download and service start. A multi-use token stays redeemable for its remaining uses and lifetime.
The attacker can reach the manager's gRPC Enroll endpoint, which the enrolling host must reach anyway.
An org admin creates a token, and an operator runs the printed install command on a host that other local users share.

execution.attacker_perspective: An unprivileged local user on a Linux host that an operator is enrolling with the printed install command, reading other processes' /proc/<pid>/cmdline.
payloads: /bin/sh -s -- --token pxa1.0190dummy-0000-7000-8000-000000000000.V14DUMMYSECRETV14DUMMYSECRET.V14PIN --manager manager.example:8444   (stdin = deploy/install.sh)
instructions: Copy the source to scratch and add a stdlib-only Go test (internal/zzargvcheck). The test starts `/bin/sh -s -- --token <dummy pxa1 token> --manager manager.example:8444` the way the printed command starts the installer, with stdin held open.

Run the test in the approved offline sandbox: network none, uid 65532, read-only root and source, all capabilities dropped, no-new-privileges, resource limits. While the shell waits for its script, stat /proc/<pid>/cmdline and /proc/<pid>/environ and read cmdline.

Write the real deploy/install.sh to the shell's stdin and close it. This shows that the real installer parses --token from argv. It stops at the root check, and the sandbox makes no network or system change.
execution.observed_result: Evidence: agents/v14-enroll-secrets/artifacts/evidence.txt (scratch evidence.txt, to be promoted). Observed: /proc/1147/cmdline mode=-r--r--r--; /proc/1147/environ mode=-r--------; cmdline="/bin/sh -s -- --token pxa1.0190dummy-0000-7000-8000-000000000000.V14DUMMYSECRETV14DUMMYSECRET.V14PIN --manager manager.example:8444 "; cmdline_contains_token=true; install.sh exit=exit status 1, output 'install.sh: must run as root (e.g. curl ... | sudo sh -s -- --token ...)'. This matches the hunter's independent run (agents/h20-enroll-secrets/artifacts/evidence.txt). The sandbox has a single uid, so no second uid actually read the file. The cross-uid readability rests on the observed 0444 procfs mode, the kernel default that only hidepid changes. Redeeming the token against a manager was not run because it needs the database. That step rests on source: Enroll at internal/agentapi/service.go:148-224 and ClaimToken at internal/agents/service.go:355.

remediation.strategy: Stop putting the secret on the command line. Print an install command without the token, and have install.sh read the token from a root-only channel: a no-echo prompt on /dev/tty, or a `--token-file` path that must be root-owned with no group or other access. Keep `--token` only as a deprecated fallback that prints a warning. The agent should keep receiving PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN only through the 0600 env file, as it does today. Make the same change to the worker docker-run snippet (internal/api/worker_snippets.go:29): prefer `--env-file` with a 0600 file over `-e PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN=...`. Update the end-user docs for the new install flow.

code_changes.fixed_code:
--token-file)
	[ $# -ge 2 ] || usage
	f="$2"; shift 2
	[ "$(stat -c '%u %a' "$f")" = "0 600" ] || die "--token-file must be owned by root with mode 600"
	PULSIX_TOKEN="$(head -n1 "$f")"
	;;
...
if [ -z "$PULSIX_TOKEN" ]; then
	[ -r /dev/tty ] || die "no terminal to read the enrollment token from; pass --token-file <root-only file>"
	printf 'Enrollment token: ' > /dev/tty
	stty -echo < /dev/tty
	IFS= read -r PULSIX_TOKEN < /dev/tty || true
	stty echo < /dev/tty
	printf '\n' > /dev/tty
fi

likelihood.reason: The attacker needs a lower-privileged local account on the very host being enrolled. With the default single-use token, the attacker must also win a short race during the install, or a multi-use token must have been created.

impact.reason: The attacker gets an org agent identity. With a host-bound token, the attacker takes over that host's agent registration: the genuine agent's enrollment is refused or its serial revoked, and the attacker controls the host's facts, auto tags, check results and heartbeats. With an unbound or multi-use token, the attacker can add monitored hosts to the org. The agent identity reaches no SSH, job or credential material, because created hosts are unmanaged and agents have no exec path.

confidence.reason: The source shows the token in the printed command's argv and the installer reading it only from argv. Two independent sandbox runs saw a 0444 cmdline file containing the token for an `sh -s -- --token` process. Enroll and ClaimToken show that any holder of the token can redeem it. The record does not claim the sudo-log copy as observed.

title: A same-site sibling origin can drive cookie-authenticated POST mutations: SameSite=Lax is the only CSRF control, and huma parses a body with no Content-Type as JSON
description: The pulsix_session cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/, has no __Host- prefix, and no anti-CSRF token or Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check exists anywhere in the manager's router chain or handlers. Lax stops cross-site requests only. A same-site origin, such as another subdomain under the manager's registrable domain, gets the cookie attached to its subresource POSTs. huma v2.39.1 (api.go Unmarshal) treats an empty Content-Type as application/json, and a local harness showed text/plain and form bodies get 415 while the same JSON body with no Content-Type runs the operation. Under the Fetch standard, a fetch() POST whose body is an ArrayBuffer or typed array sends no Content-Type, so it is a CORS simple request that needs no preflight. Script on a less-trusted same-site host could therefore make a logged-in victim's browser run any POST operation the victim's role allows, without reading the response. For example, an admin victim could be made to invite an attacker-chosen email address at up to admin role. tenancy.Invite refuses only owner, and mails the accept link to that address, so the attacker joins the org. PUT, PATCH and DELETE routes need a preflight and are not reachable this way. Separately, without __Host- a sibling host can set a same-named cookie scoped to the parent domain. After backlog 7.19 it can no longer fix the victim's own session, but it can still log the victim's browser into an attacker-controlled account. Cross-site attackers stay blocked by Lax.
claimed_root_cause: sessionCookie (internal/api/auth_handlers.go:159-161) relies on SameSite=Lax alone and uses the unprefixed name pulsix_session (internal/auth/middleware.go:13). The api.New middleware chain (internal/api/api.go:369-403: RequestID/Logger/Recoverer, securityHeaders, staticSessionSkip(CookieMiddleware), requireMFAForExplorer) has no Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site or token check for cookie-authenticated unsafe methods, and does not use http.CrossOriginProtection. huma.DefaultConfig is used unchanged for formats (api.go:433), and huma v2.39.1 api.Unmarshal falls back to application/json when Content-Type is empty, so the 415 for text/plain and form types does not stop a POST with no Content-Type.

trace.description: The session cookie is issued as pulsix_session with Path=/, HttpOnly, Secure only when PublicURL is https, and SameSite=Lax, with no __Host- prefix. A browser attaches it to any same-site request, including a subresource POST from a sibling-subdomain page, which is the lower-trust entry.
The first cookie named pulsix_session is resolved to the victim principal. Nothing about the request origin is consulted.

The router-level middleware is securityHeaders, then the session lookup, then requireMFAForExplorer (line 403). None checks Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site or a CSRF token for unsafe methods. huma.DefaultConfig at line 433 keeps huma's empty-Content-Type-to-JSON fallback.

title: An API token that may not mint tokens can still mint an admin membership that survives its revocation
description: POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/tokens refuses a bearer-token principal ('credentials do not mint credentials'), so that a leaked token cannot outlive its own revocation through a successor it created. The member routes on the same bearer-enabled org-scoped group do not apply that rule. A token whose effective role is admin or owner can call POST /orgs/{org}/invites with role admin. When outgoing mail is not configured, the response returns accept_url. When mail is configured, the holder can invite an address it controls. The same token can PATCH /orgs/{org}/members/{userId} to promote an existing member it controls to admin. The invited or promoted account is an ordinary interactive identity. Revoking the leaked token does not affect it. An invite stays redeemable for 7 days (InviteTTL), and no route lists or cancels pending invites. Once its holder enrols a second factor, the successor's MFA-complete session can mint new admin API tokens. Owner cannot be granted through this path: the invite schema excludes it, and ChangeRole requires an owner actor role, which the admin cap prevents. Calibration, not demonstrated here: the same token-only gating applies to other durable credentials, including trigger secrets, agent enrollment tokens and worker enrollment tokens. The membership variant is the strongest because it yields a full interactive admin identity.
root_cause: The 'no successor credential from a bearer token' rule is enforced only by requireInteractiveSession inside the POST /tokens handler. The invite, member-role and member-removal handlers are registered on the same bearer-enabled org-scoped group but authorize with requireOrg(PermMembersManage) alone. requireOrg checks role, not principal kind. tenancy.Service.Invite and AcceptInvite do not tie an invitation's validity to the credential that issued it or to the issuer's continued authority. PeekInvite and TakeInvite check only the hash, acceptance and expiry.
intended_behavior: A bearer token must not create an identity or credential that outlives its revocation, as token_handlers.go already states for token minting. Creating invites and changing member roles should require an interactive, MFA-complete session, the same as POST /tokens. Alternatively, an invite created through a token should be bound to that token and voided when the token is revoked. Admins should also be able to list and cancel pending invites.

trace.description: The org-scoped group mounts bearerAuthMiddleware, then orgScopeMiddleware (line 541). registerMemberRoutes (line 543) and registerTokenRoutes (line 544) are registered on this group, so a pxt_ bearer token reaches the member and invite routes.
A resolved token becomes a Principal with TokenID set and MFAComplete=true, plus a TokenScope that carries the token's org and role.
Control: token creation calls requireInteractiveSession, which refuses any principal with TokenID != nil (auth_handlers.go:257). No member or invite handler has this control.
The invite handler only calls requireOrg(PermMembersManage), then deps.Tenancy.Invite with the requested role. The schema allows admin, operator or viewer.
The token cap lowers the role to Lower(membership, token role). An admin cap still satisfies members.manage (roles.go:91), and no check on principal kind follows.

When the mailer returns mail.ErrNotConfigured, the invite is stored with InvitedBy set to the token owner, and the plaintext accept link is returned to the bearer caller. Nothing records which credential created the invite.
Same gate: requireOrg(PermMembersManage) only. ChangeRole (service.go:521) guards only the owner role against a non-owner actor, so an admin-capped token can promote any non-owner member to admin.

After the issuing token is revoked, PeekInvite and TakeInvite (tenancy_users.sql:65-81) still find the invite by hash, acceptance and expiry, and AddMembership grants the invite's admin role to the new account.

evidence.description: The stated invariant (lines 89-92): 'a bearer token can list and revoke tokens but never mint one, so a leaked credential cannot outlive its own revocation through a successor it created.'
POST /orgs/{org}/invites is gated only by requireOrg(ctx, deps, in.Org, tenancy.PermMembersManage), with no requireInteractiveSession.
The invite body accepts role enum admin, operator or viewer.

PeekInvite and TakeInvite match only token_hash, accepted_at IS NULL and expires_at > now. They have no link to the issuing credential or to the issuer's current authority. internal/api registers only two invite routes: POST /orgs/{org}/invites and POST /invites/accept. No route lists or deletes invites.
requireInteractiveSession exists. Its only callers are token creation, the passkey and MFA account routes, and requireInstanceAdmin (authz.go:112). Membership management does not call it.
InviteTTL is 7 * 24h, so an invite created by the token stays redeemable for a week after the token is revoked.

conditions.description: The attacker holds a valid pxt_ API token whose effective role (the lower of the token's role and its owner's live membership role) is admin or owner in the target org. An example is a leaked CI or automation token. Viewer and operator tokens fail members.manage.
To get the accept link directly in the response, the instance has no outgoing mail configured. With mail configured, the attacker invites an address it controls instead.
The promotion variant needs an existing non-owner member account that the attacker controls.
The invite must be accepted within its 7-day TTL. Acceptance can happen after the token is revoked.

title: Second-factor guessing on /auth/totp/verify is limited only per source address, so a password holder can brute-force the TOTP code
description: POST /api/v1/auth/totp/verify is the only step between a password-only (pending) session and an MFA-complete session for a TOTP account. The only bound on wrong codes is the per-address auth limiter: by default 20 failures per minute per IPv4 address or per IPv6 /64, per endpoint. Nothing counts failures per account or per session, and a wrong code neither revokes nor marks the pending session. An attacker who has the victim's password can log in (successful logins are refunded by the limiter), keep the pending session for up to 12 h (renewable by logging in again), and send six-digit guesses from as many source keys as they control. Three codes are valid at any instant (current step plus or minus one), so each guess succeeds with probability about 3e-6. One IPv4 address gives 28,800 guesses a day, about an 8% chance per day; a routed IPv6 /56 (256 /64 keys) gives 5,120 guesses a minute and an expected success in about an hour. A correct guess upgrades the session to MFA-complete with a fresh cookie, which is full account takeover including the victim's org roles and any instance-admin flag. Backlog 7.8 fixed the run-1 concurrency bypass and explicitly lists a per-account second-factor failure counter as not done.
root_cause: authRateLimitMiddleware (internal/api/auth_rate_limit.go:74-91) keys its budget only on the resolved client address via clientip.Limiter.Reserve (internal/clientip/limiter.go:105-127), whose key() counts IPv4 per address and IPv6 per /64 (limiter.go:165-174). The verify handler (internal/api/mfa_handlers.go:164-178), verifyFactorCode (mfa_handlers.go:50-67) and TOTP.Verify/verifyAndConsume (internal/auth/totp.go:229-296) keep no failed-attempt state per user or per session; the only TOTP write on the path is SetTOTPLastStep, on success (internal/db/queries/auth.sql:83), and no failure counter exists in the schema or queries. The total guess budget against one account therefore grows linearly with attacker source keys and time.
intended_behavior: Wrong second-factor attempts against one account (or one pending session) should be bounded regardless of how many source addresses send them: after a small number of consecutive failures the pending session is revoked and further verification for that user is locked or exponentially delayed, so a stolen password alone cannot be turned into an MFA-complete session by guessing.

trace.description: Attacker with the victim's password obtains a pending (mfa_complete=false) session cookie via Auth.Login (sessions.Create(..., false)); a successful login is refunded by the limiter and can be repeated to renew the 12 h session.
lim.Reserve(ip) is the only budget check: keyed on the resolved client address alone, so each new IPv4 address or IPv6 /64 starts a fresh 20/min window for the same session and account.
requireSession admits the pending session; verifyFactorCode checks the guess and returns 401 on a wrong code with no per-user or per-session failure accounting and no session revocation.
matchStep accepts the code of the current step or either neighbouring step; a wrong code returns (false, nil) and nothing is recorded.
The first correct guess upgrades the attacker's session to MFA-complete and returns its new session cookie.

evidence.description: key(): IPv4 per address, IPv6 per /64; the only dimension the auth limiter counts on.
DefaultAuthRateLimit = 20 failed attempts per minute per address per endpoint.
totpSkewSteps = 1: three six-digit codes are valid at any instant.
SetTOTPLastStep is the only TOTP write on the verify path, and only on success; no failure counter column or query exists.
SessionTTL = 12 h: lifetime of the pending session the guesses run against.
Backlog 7.8 closure note: 'Not done: a per-account second-factor failure counter independent of the address.'

Guess rate scales with distinct source keys the manager sees: one IPv4 address gives 20/min (about 8%/day); an IPv6 /56 or a pool of addresses gives thousands per minute. Requires the manager to see the true client address (direct exposure, or PULSIX_TRUSTED_PROXIES set for the fronting proxy); behind an untrusted proxy all callers share one key and the global rate is 20/min.
Victim account uses TOTP as its second factor. A passkey-only account has no TOTP secret and Verify always fails; recovery codes are 80-bit and not guessable.
Success is probabilistic per guess (about 3e-6); expected effort is about 333k guesses.

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of a dummy victim's password but not the authenticator, sending /auth/totp/verify guesses for one pending session from many source addresses.

remediation.strategy: Add a per-user (or per pending session) failed second-factor counter in the database (additive migration) and check it before verifying. Increment it atomically on every failed TOTP or recovery-code check through verifyFactorCode, on the verify and the disable path. Keep the per-address limiter as the outer layer and audit-log lockouts.

impact.reason: Defeats the second factor and yields an MFA-complete session for the victim: all org roles, credential and job access, and instance-admin powers if the victim holds them.
