Only the DB-backed stores were faked; their SQL (auth.sql) has no failure state, and the owner's backlog records the per-account counter as not implemented.

title: Worker enrollment token placed in docker CLI argv on the worker host before redemption
description: When an org admin adds a worker, the API returns a docker run snippet that passes the one-time worker enrollment token (id, secret and CA pin, pxw1 format) as `-e PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN=<token>`. The README tells admins to run that command on the worker machine. The token therefore sits in the docker CLI's command line for as long as that process runs. With `-d` the CLI exits once the container has started, but on a fresh worker host it first pulls the noixdev/pulsix-worker image, which takes seconds to minutes. The container redeems the token only after it starts. On a Linux host where /proc is mounted without hidepid, another local account that is not root and not in the docker group can read /proc/<pid>/cmdline during that window. It can then call the anonymous Enroll RPC (rate-limited per IP, needs no client certificate) with the token and a CSR for its own key. Redemption checks only the secret hash, that the token is unused and that it has not expired. The manager signs the attacker's CSR for the org, zone and worker name the admin chose and marks the token used in the same transaction. The legitimate container's Enroll is then refused, and its restarts are refused too. The rogue holder of the certificate is an authenticated zone worker. It can claim that zone's jobs and receive the decrypted credentials they carry until an admin notices and revokes it. The audit entry 'enrolled from <ip>' shows the worker host's own address, so it does not reveal the swap. The compose variant writes the token into a YAML file whose permissions the snippet leaves to the admin's umask; that file is exposed until `docker compose up` redeems the token. Source fully establishes the code path. Whether a lower-trust local reader exists on supported worker hosts is a deployment fact. This is the same pattern as, but a separate code path from, the agent installer one-liner (`curl … | sudo sh -s -- --token …`, internal/api/agent_handlers.go:349).
claimed_root_cause: workerSnippets renders the one-time secret as a docker `-e NAME=value` command-line argument (internal/api/worker_snippets.go:29) and not through a channel only the admin can read (for example `--env-file` pointing at a 0600 file, or `-e PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN` with no value, inherited from a variable set by `read -s`). The token is also not bound to anything only the intended host holds, so whoever reads it from process metadata first can redeem it (internal/workers/enroll.go:153).

trace.description: Anonymous Enroll RPC, the one worker method callable without a client certificate and limited only per IP. The local attacker on the worker host calls it with the token id and secret scraped from docker CLI argv, plus a CSR for its own key.
An admin (workers.write) creates a 1-hour single-use token. The response returns the token and embeds it in the docker and compose snippets (line 232).

The token is rendered as `  -e PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN=<token> \` in the docker run command the admin runs on the worker host, which puts it in the docker CLI's argv for the CLI's lifetime, including any image pull.
The only checks are a constant-time compare of SHA-256(secret), that the token is unused and that it has not expired. Nothing ties redemption to the intended host or key.

SignCSR signs the presenter's CSR for the token's org, zone and name. The worker row, the certificate and the used mark are written in one transaction, and grpcsrv/enroll.go:54 returns the certificate to the attacker.

evidence.description: The docker snippet puts the secret on the command line: fmt.Sprintf("  -e PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN=%s \\", token). No --env-file or stdin variant exists (repo-wide grep finds no env-file use).
The compose variant writes the token into a compose file. The snippet does not constrain that file's permissions.
The documented remote-worker flow tells admins to run the printed docker run command (lines 176-181, including -e PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN=pxw1.…) on the worker's machine.
The token string carries the enrollment id, the raw 32-byte secret and the CA pin, which is everything a third party needs to redeem it.
Enroll's only gate before redemption is a per-IP rate limit of 10 per minute. A co-located attacker needs one call.

The legitimate worker's own Enroll call (ensureIdentity) runs only after the container has started, which is after any image pull, so a fast reader wins the race. When it loses, line 97 returns 'the manager refused enrollment'.
Calibration: the agent installer stores its token under umask 077 in a 0600 env file. The project uses a restricted file for at-rest storage there, but the worker snippet has no equivalent.

blockers: Whether worker hosts in supported deployments have local accounts with less authority than the admin running docker (not root, not in the docker group, not able to sudo) is a deployment fact that source does not show. Without such an account no trust boundary is crossed, because root and docker-group users are already root-equivalent on the host.

Whether /proc is mounted with hidepid=1/2 or invisible (or the host otherwise restricts /proc/<pid>/cmdline) is a host fact. So is how long the docker CLI lives on a first run (the image pull duration). Running docker run on the host is forbidden for this verifier, and the approved sandbox has a single uid, so it cannot model a second OS user.
Whether the attacker account can reach the manager's gRPC worker endpoint from the worker host is a network-policy fact. The worker host itself must reach it, so it is normally reachable.

validation_plan.local: On a disposable Linux VM with default /proc mount options (no hidepid), no network access beyond a local dummy registry, and a dummy unprivileged user 'probe' that is not in the docker group: (1) as the docker-capable admin, remove any local copy of the worker image, then run the snippet exactly as workerSnippets renders it, with a dummy token value such as pxw1.DUMMY and a manager address that does not resolve; (2) while it pulls, have 'probe' run a bounded loop for at most 120 s (grep -a -l 'PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN=pxw1.DUMMY' /proc/[0-9]*/cmdline). Record only whether 'probe' saw the dummy value and for how many seconds. Redeem nothing, contact no real manager, and destroy the VM afterwards. Repeat once with the image already present to record the short-window case.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed, read-only, on a real worker host: (a) getent passwd and getent group docker to list interactive accounts that are neither root nor in docker or sudo; (b) grep ' /proc ' /proc/mounts to check for hidepid/subset options; (c) confirm whether worker hosts are documented or provisioned as single-tenant appliances. If lower-trust accounts exist and /proc is not restricted, the finding holds as described.

title: Workers added from the Workers page run playbooks as the worker uid, so a playbook can read the worker's mTLS key
description: The docker run and compose snippets that the Add worker dialog prints do not set PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID, and the worker image deliberately leaves it unset. Every worker started from those snippets therefore loads PlayUID=0. newRunnerCmd then starts ansible-runner and the play as the worker's own uid 65532 instead of through the setuid helper. That uid owns the 0700 identity directory and the 0600 key.pem that token enrollment writes under the data volume. A localhost task in any playbook run on that worker can read the worker's client key and certificate. The bundled compose worker sets PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID=65533 to prevent this. The play-uid design names this theft as the exposure the feature closes: with the key, the code becomes the worker and can claim further jobs of the same organization and zone. For a malicious operator-level member, the key adds three things to the code execution they already have by design. They can act as the zone's worker from any host that reaches the manager's worker gRPC endpoint. They can claim jobs that other members launch and receive those jobs' credentials, and they can report forged results. That access survives their removal from the organization until an admin revokes the worker.
root_cause: workerSnippets (internal/api/worker_snippets.go:21-47) emits only PULSIX_MANAGER_ADDR, PULSIX_MANAGER_SERVER_NAME and PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN. It never emits PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID=65533. The image intentionally leaves that variable unset (deploy/worker/Dockerfile:151-159) so that existing deployments must opt in, and config.Load sets PlayUID only when the variable is present (internal/worker/config.go:230-248). The design makes the separation opt-in only to protect existing deployments. That reason does not apply to a fresh worker started from the official image, which the snippet always describes, yet the UI path never opts in.
intended_behavior: A worker started from the Add worker snippet is always a fresh installation of the official image, which ships uid 65533 and the setuid helper. It should run playbooks under the separate play uid, as the bundled compose worker does, so that a localhost task cannot read the worker's identity directory.

trace.description: An organization member with jobs.run (operator, roles.go:114) runs a job template whose playbook contains a localhost task. The ad-hoc command route (adhoc_handlers.go:48) and playbook or repo writes (operator) are equivalent entries.

When an admin (workers.write) adds the worker on the Workers page, the response carries the docker and compose snippets that workerSnippets returns. This is the documented way to add a remote worker (deploy/compose/README.md:171).
The docker run snippet (lines 25-32) and the compose snippet (lines 33-47) set only MANAGER_ADDR, MANAGER_SERVER_NAME and ENROLL_TOKEN. Neither sets PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID.
The image deliberately leaves PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID unset (lines 151-159). Its only ENV is PULSIX_WORKER_DATA_DIR (line 148), and it runs as USER 65532:65532 (line 161).
PlayUID is set only when PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID is present, so a worker started from the snippet keeps PlayUID=0.
Token enrollment writes key.pem with mode 0600 into <data dir>/identity, which is created 0700 at line 65. Both are owned by the worker uid 65532.
newRunnerCmd prepends the setuid helper only when PlayUID != 0. With PlayUID=0, the supervisor, ansible-runner and the play run as the worker uid, and a localhost task can read key.pem.

evidence.description: The snippet's env lines. PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID is never emitted. In a local test, a verbatim copy of this function fed to worker.Load gave PlayUID=0.
The bundled worker sets PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID to 65533 so that a task aimed at the worker cannot read its certificate and key (comment at lines 177-185).
The README says playbooks do not run as the worker. Its remote-worker section (lines 156-186) points administrators to the UI snippet, which does not enable that separation.
The PlayUID field comment says that with PlayUID 0 a localhost task runs as the worker, which can read the worker's own client certificate and key.

The design names theft of the worker certificate ("it IS that worker, and can claim further jobs ... it was never given") as the exposure to close. It makes the separation opt-in only so that existing deployments keep working.
The sweep between jobs, and the rest of the play-uid hardening, are also skipped when PlayUID==0.

conditions.description: The attacker is an organization member with jobs.run, playbooks.write or repos.write (operator or higher) who can run a playbook that lands on the affected zone's worker.
An admin started the worker from the Add worker docker run or compose snippet and did not add PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID by hand. This is the default UI path.
Using the stolen key from outside the worker requires network reach to the manager's worker gRPC endpoint. Remote UI-enrolled workers already require that endpoint to be published.

execution.attacker_perspective: An organization operator whose playbook runs on a worker that an admin added through the Workers page.
payloads: A scratch package containing a body-identical copy of internal/api/worker_snippets.go. Its docker snippet's -e variables, plus the image ENV PULSIX_WORKER_DATA_DIR=/var/lib/pulsix-worker, are passed to worker.Load. Dummy inputs: token pxw1.dummy, address manager.invalid:8444.

A playbook with hosts: localhost, connection: local and the task `command: cat /var/lib/pulsix-worker/identity/key.pem`, run in noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev against a dummy 0600 key.pem in a 0700 identity directory owned by 65532 (on a tmpfs data volume).
instructions: Test 1, offline Go sandbox (--network none, read-only source and module cache, uid 65532): run go test -run TestV19SnippetPlayUID ./internal/zzv19/ and read the RESULT lines for the PlayUID that the snippet-configured worker loads.

Test 2, offline worker-image sandbox variant (--network none --read-only, with resource limits, image USER 65532): write the dummy key with mode 0600, run ansible-playbook -i localhost, on the playbook above as the image user, which is the PlayUID=0 path. Then run /usr/local/bin/pulsix-setuid-exec 65533 /usr/bin/cat on the same file, which is the PlayUID=65533 path, for contrast.
execution.observed_result: Test 1: 'RESULT snippet worker PlayUID=0 KeyPath=/var/lib/pulsix-worker/identity/key.pem', 'RESULT docker mentions PLAY_UID=false compose mentions PLAY_UID=false', and with the bundled compose value 'PlayUID=65533' (agents/v19-worker-token/artifacts/evidence.txt). Test 2: the image runs as uid=65532(pulsix), and the identity directory is drwx------ pulsix with key.pem -rw------- pulsix. The localhost play printed 'RESULT play uid read: DUMMY-V19-NOT-A-KEY' (ok=2 failed=0). Through the helper as 65533, cat returned 'Permission denied' (exit 1) (agents/v19-worker-token/artifacts/evidence2.txt). Not executed: a real enrolled worker claiming a job, and any use of a key.

remediation.strategy: Emit PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID=65533 in both generated snippets. The snippet always names the official noixdev/pulsix-worker image on a fresh named volume, so the opt-in reasoning for existing deployments does not apply. Update the README's remote-worker example to match. Extend worker_snippets_test.go to assert that both snippets carry the variable. Do not add no-new-privileges to the snippet, because the setuid helper needs it off.

code_changes.fixed_code:
fmt.Sprintf("  -e PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN=%s \\", token),
		"  -e PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID=65533 \\",
		...
		fmt.Sprintf("      PULSIX_ENROLL_TOKEN: %q", token),
		`      PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID: "65533"`,

likelihood.reason: Every UI-enrolled worker is affected by default, but exploitation needs a malicious operator-level member. It also adds value over powers the operator already has by design only through persistence, impersonation, or claiming other members' jobs.

impact.reason: The attacker steals the worker's mTLS identity, which the design names as protected. They can then act as the zone's worker: claim jobs other members launch and receive their credentials, and forge results. This lasts beyond the member's removal until an admin revokes the worker. It is limited to one organization and zone.

confidence.reason: Both halves were observed locally against target source and the target-equivalent image. The snippet produces PlayUID=0, and a localhost play running as the image's worker uid read a 0600 key in the 0700 identity directory, while the 65533 helper path was denied. The link between them (newRunnerCmd skips the helper when PlayUID=0) is direct source. A full enrolled-worker job run was not executed.

title: One odd mount point on a monitored host makes the manager refuse every disk sample from that host and keeps cutting its agent connection
description: When no 'mounts' list is configured (the seeded default), the agent's disk plugin reports every mount point it finds in /proc/1/mountinfo as a check item, unchanged. The only filter is a pseudo-filesystem one (tmpfs, devtmpfs, overlay, squashfs), so FUSE mounts are included. gopsutil reverses the kernel's octal escaping with strconv.Unquote, so a TAB or newline in a directory name reaches the item as a real control character. The manager's ingest contract refuses the whole CheckResults message if any single item is longer than 512 bytes or contains a control character. agentapi then ends the AgentStream with InvalidArgument. The hunter's sandboxed test (agents/h21-tenant-availability/artifacts/evidence2.txt) shows this: one batch held a valid cpu sample, a valid '/' disk sample and one bad mount item, the client Send returned nil, the stream ended with InvalidArgument and 0 of 3 samples were stored. The agent has no length cap, escaping or skip for these items. The shipped unit sets ProtectHome=true, but that does not help: if the agent cannot stat the mount, the plugin still sends error observations under the same item. The result is that every disk interval (5 min in the seed) drops all of that host's disk samples, including the '/' usage that disk-full alerting relies on, and cuts the stream. The reconnect backoff only resets after a clean session end, so it climbs to the 60 s cap. sendResultsChunked counts a chunk as sent once the client-side Send returns, so results replayed from the disconnect buffer in chunks of 200 are lost too when a chunk also holds the bad disk result, along with any cpu, memory and service samples buffered with it. The effect is limited to the host that carries the mount, within its own organization. It would be a security issue if an unprivileged local user on a monitored host can create such a mount in init's mount namespace, for example a FUSE/sshfs mount through setuid fusermount3 at a path over 512 bytes or with a TAB in it. Whether they can depends on the OS and its packages, which this repository does not show. A second trigger exists on the manager side: an operator-entered disk 'mounts' entry over 512 bytes or with a control character passes validateParams and is refused at ingest in the same way. That case is an operator misconfiguration, not a privilege boundary.
claimed_root_cause: The check-results item contract (at most 512 bytes, no control or line-separator characters) is enforced only at manager ingest. It is an all-or-nothing batch refusal that also ends the agent stream (samples.go:283-286, stream.go:266-275 and 106-111). The design comment (samples.go:102-125) knows that items are mount points, but it treats any violation as 'the agent is broken or lying'. It does not consider that a mount point, which the host discovers, can legitimately exceed 512 bytes or contain a TAB or newline that gopsutil has unescaped. stream.go:107-110 assumes 'the agent's own collector normalizes', but disk.go:84/99 pass mount points through unchanged. Manager-side validateParams (definitions.go:154-158) rejects only empty 'mounts' entries. Nothing on the path normalizes, escapes, skips or isolates a single bad item, and the agent treats chunks the server refused as delivered.

trace.description: Each mount point from gopsutil disk.PartitionsWithContext (/proc/1/mountinfo, unescaped with strconv.Unquote in gopsutil v4.26.8 disk_unix.go:57 and disk_linux.go:314/421) is added to the candidate list unchanged. The only filter is pseudoFilesystems (tmpfs, devtmpfs, overlay, squashfs), so fuse.* mounts pass.

The mount point becomes Observation.Item for three metrics. This happens both when Usage fails (lines 117-119, for example a mount the ProtectHome=true agent namespace cannot reach) and when it succeeds (lines 127-129).

trace.scope: Scheduler run loop for one check
trace.description: Every interval, the whole Collect output is converted to Results (Item unchanged) and passed to the session sink.
Item is copied to the wire unchanged. sendResultsChunked (lines 106-117) counts a chunk as sent as soon as the client Send returns nil.
The whole message is passed to checks.Service.RecordObservations. ErrInvalidInput is wrapped as errCheckResultsRejected (line 275).

withinContract fails on the one item (len > MaxItemLen at line 184, or breaksLine at line 188). The whole batch is refused before the shape and plausibility checks that work per item, and before the store is called.
errCheckResultsRejected becomes codes.InvalidArgument and the AgentStream ends. Every observation in the message is lost, and the agent's heartbeat and facts session ends with it.

evidence.description: Design premise: every field comes from manager config or a compile-time constant, so a violation means 'the agent is broken or lying'. Lines 122-125 acknowledge that items are disk mount points but assume 512 bytes covers them, and do not consider control characters.
MaxItemLen = 512, enforced as a refusal of the whole batch.
Comment assumes 'the agent's own collector normalizes'. The disk collector does not.
An explicit 'mounts' param is also used unchanged as items. This is the manager-side trigger.
pseudoFilesystems filters only tmpfs, devtmpfs, overlay and squashfs. FUSE mounts are reported.

activateSender replays the disconnect buffer through sendResultsChunked. Chunks the server later refuses count as sent and are not re-buffered, so co-buffered cpu, memory and service samples are lost with them.
Backoff resets only after a clean session end. Repeated InvalidArgument cuts climb to maxBackoff = 60 s (loop.go:49).
Manager-side disk 'mounts' validation rejects only empty or whitespace entries, not length or control characters.
The seeded disk check is enabled for the whole org every 5 minutes with no 'mounts' param, so discovery is the default path.

ProtectHome=true, with no CapabilityBoundingSet (root keeps access to /proc/1 under ProtectProc=invisible). Home mounts are still listed from init's mountinfo, and a Usage failure still sends the item as an error observation.

blockers: Can an unprivileged local user on a supported Linux distribution create a mount in init's mount namespace whose path is longer than 512 bytes or contains a TAB or newline, for example sshfs/FUSE through setuid fusermount3 in a directory they own, or udisks automount of removable media with a crafted label? That is an OS and package fact outside the repository, and it decides whether this is a privilege-boundary issue. Without it, the trigger is root, an operator misconfiguration, or an accidental long or odd mount path.

The approved sandbox's module cache (volume pulsix-gomodcache) has no github.com/shirou/gopsutil (checked: /go/pkg/mod/github.com/shirou/gopsutil and its cache/download directory are both missing). internal/agent and internal/agent/checks therefore cannot be built under the required -mod=readonly GOPROXY=off controls, so disk.Partitions -> diskPlugin.Collect -> Loop replay could not be run end to end. That part rests on source plus the hunter's verbatim copy of unescapeFstab (agents/h21-tenant-availability/artifacts/evidence.txt).

validation_plan.local: Add github.com/shirou/gopsutil/v4 v4.26.8 and its go.sum dependencies to the read-only sandbox module cache. Then, in a scratch copy, add a test in internal/agent/checks that runs diskPlugin{Partitions: gopsutilPartitions{}, Usage: fakeUsage} with HOST_PROC_MOUNTINFO set to a fixture mountinfo file. The file should have a '/' line, a fuse.sshfs line mounted at '/home/u/a\011b', and a fuse.sshfs line with a 600-byte mount point. Assert that the items contain '\t' and a len>512 string. Feed those Results through internal/agent's Loop against a fake Stream whose Recv returns status InvalidArgument after the CheckResults Send. Assert three things: streamSession returns an error, the buffer does not get the refused chunk back, and backoffShift keeps growing to maxBackoff. Pair this with the existing agentapi test (evidence2) showing 0 of N stored.
validation_plan.deployment: Use a disposable test VM running the installed agent (the shipped systemd unit) with the default seeded checks, enrolled into a test org. As an unprivileged user with fuse3 and sshfs installed, try fusermount3/sshfs mounts at (a) a directory under $HOME whose absolute path is 520 bytes long and (b) a directory whose name contains a TAB. Record whether fusermount3 accepts each one. If it does, cat /proc/1/mountinfo, then watch the manager's host page for the next 5-minute disk interval and the agent journal for 'agent stream failed ... InvalidArgument'. Repeat with udisks automount of a USB image whose filesystem label has a TAB or is very long, if the distro auto-mounts. Unmount afterwards. Read-only observation, no load.

title: Host-tag selectors have no length or condition limit and become one huge SQL statement on the shared pool
description: selector.Parse accepts any number of 'and'-joined conditions, and Selector.SQL compiles each one 1:1 into a correlated EXISTS / NOT EXISTS sub-query over the host_tags CTE, all in a single statement sent on the manager's one shared pgx pool. The only source-visible bounds are huma's default 1 MiB request body and pgx's 65535 bind-parameter limit: a 845010-byte JSON body carries 65000 'k exists' conditions, which render into a 5253893-byte SQL fragment with 65000 EXISTS sub-queries and 65001 bind parameters (reproduced locally in the sandbox). Any viewer reaches this per request through POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/hosts/query (hosts.read) and POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/monitoring-groups/preview (checks.read); since any MFA-complete user may create an organization and become its owner, any logged-in user can also store such a selector in a monitoring group of their own org, after which it is re-executed on every agent heartbeat's ResolveHost (once per group), on group pushes and in the fleet / rule-state group filters. Neither the code nor the shipped compose DSN sets statement_timeout or pool_max_conns, so the pool defaults to max(4, NumCPU) connections and Postgres to no statement timeout; a few slow statements could occupy the pool and database CPU/memory shared by every tenant. Whether PostgreSQL planning of thousands of pulled-up semi/anti-joins is actually expensive (or fails fast, e.g. on max_stack_depth for very deep join trees) has not been measured.
claimed_root_cause: Neither the selector grammar (parser.go:56-72), the request DTOs (tag_handlers.go:90 has only minLength:1; monitoring_group_handlers.go:37 and :67 have no constraint), checks.normalize (groups.go:240-243) nor checks.Preview (groups.go:337) bound selector length or condition count before Selector.SQL (selector.go:184-219) compiles it into one EXISTS sub-query per condition that hosts.SQLStore.QueryHosts executes as a single statement with no per-query deadline.

trace.description: Viewer-supplied selector (hosts.read, body up to huma's default 1 MiB) is parsed with no size or condition limit.
Every 'and'-joined condition is appended without bound.
sel.SQL(1) renders one correlated EXISTS / NOT EXISTS sub-query per condition, AND-ed into the WHERE clause of a query over a host_tags CTE.
The single statement (up to ~65000 sub-queries / 65001 parameters) is executed on the shared pool with the request context as the only deadline.

evidence.description: Each 'k exists' condition becomes EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM host_tags t WHERE t.host_id = h.id AND t.key = $n); opEq/opNeq/opIn produce the same shape (lines 198, 204, 214).
hostQueryInput.Selector carries only minLength:1, no maxLength.
Preview of an arbitrary, unsaved selector needs only checks.read (viewer, line 222); the body DTO at line 67 has no constraint.
Stored group selectors are validated only by selector.Parse, with no length or condition limit; the text column (migration 00042) is unconstrained and unindexed.
Every stored group selector is re-executed (MatchingHosts -> QueryHosts) on each ResolveHost, which the agent stream runs on every heartbeat.
Stored selectors are also parsed and compiled into the fleet / rule-state query.
Any MFA-complete user can create an organization and become its owner, so storing an oversized selector needs no pre-existing operator role anywhere.
Pool configuration comes only from the DSN; no statement_timeout, MaxConns or per-query deadline is applied in code (scope.go sets only pulsix.org_id).

The shipped DSN sets neither statement_timeout nor pool_max_conns, and the db service (timescale/timescaledb:2.30.0-pg18) passes no server-side timeout, so pgxpool defaults to max(4, NumCPU) connections with no statement timeout.

blockers: The decisive cost, PostgreSQL parse/plan/execute time and memory for one statement with 1000 to 65000 correlated EXISTS sub-queries (pulled up into nested semi-joins) over a materialized CTE, cannot be measured: DB-backed execution is forbidden in this sandbox. Source analysis cannot settle it because the planner may either spend superlinear time in join planning or fail fast (for example on max_stack_depth at large nesting depths), so the worst case may sit at an intermediate size.

Whether real deployments outside the shipped compose file set statement_timeout (DSN, role or postgresql.conf), a pool size, or a reverse-proxy body cap below 1 MiB on these routes is deployment configuration outside the repository.

validation_plan.local: On a disposable local Postgres/TimescaleDB 18 container (no network, statement_timeout = '30s', memory-limited container) loaded with the migrations, create one organization with 100 hosts and 5 tags each, then through the pulsix_app role with pulsix.org_id set run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, SUMMARY) and plain EXPLAIN (planning only) on QueryHosts's exact statement for selectors of 100, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000 and 65000 'k exists' conditions, and again for 'k != v' (anti-join) conditions. Record planning time, execution time, peak backend memory and any error (e.g. stack depth limit exceeded) per size, and stop increasing size at the first case that exceeds 5 s or 512 MB. A single size that holds a backend for many seconds confirms the issue; uniform fast failure or sub-second times at all sizes refutes it.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks whether production DSNs, the pulsix_app role or postgresql.conf set statement_timeout and pool_max_conns, and whether any reverse proxy in front of the manager caps request bodies below 1 MiB for /api/v1/orgs/*/hosts/query, /api/v1/orgs/*/monitoring-groups/preview and the monitoring-group create/update routes.

title: Key rotation installs, verifies and revokes on the credential's username, not on the account runs log in as, so the old key stays valid there
description: Ordinary runs pick the SSH login user from the host's own SSH settings first and fall back to the credential's username (render.go:369-372). ProxyJump hops always dial bastion.Username (chain.go:60). The rotation group does the opposite: rotate_key, its follow-up connection_test and revoke_key all use the credential's username first (system_claim.go:467-470 and 186-189, queue_sql.go:907-908). On a bastion target, bastion.Username is ignored whenever the credential has a username. Take a host or jump host whose run account (for example deploy@web1 or jumper@jump-01) differs from the credential's non-empty username (for example ansible), and where the old key K1 also authenticates the credential's account. That happens, for example, when bootstrap installed K1 for pulsix_user = the credential username and the operator added K1 to the run account by hand. In that case the rotation installs K2 for 'ansible', verifies K2 as 'ansible', seals K2 onto the credential (FinishRotation), and then removes K1 from 'ansible' only. The account Pulsix actually manages the host through keeps K1 and never receives K2. The rotation group reports success and the revocation completes, yet the retired (possibly leaked) key still authenticates as the managed account. Afterwards every run and the daily connection test against that target fail, because the credential now holds K2 and the run account never got it. The operator therefore sees a breakage, but nothing tells them that K1 is still authorized there. Restoring access needs a manual fix on the target or a new bootstrap with a one-time login. If K1 does not authenticate the credential's account, rotate_key fails and nothing changes (fail-safe).
root_cause: The code resolves the username in two independent places, with opposite precedence. render.hostVars (render.go:369-372) uses ssh.Username first, then CredentialUsers[credential]. Hop dials use bastion.Username (render.go:385 via sshconf.ProxyJump, chain.go:60). rotateKindPayload (system_claim.go:467-470) and revokeKindPayload (system_claim.go:186-189) use cred.Username first and fall back to the rendered or bastion username only when it is empty. The worker uses that value both as the SSH login and as the authorized_key user (rotate.go:71-81, the playbooks' pulsix_user). The rotation verification probe also replaces the rendered ansible_user (queue_sql.go:887) with cred.Username (queue_sql.go:907-908). So the all-succeeded gate in recordRotation checks the credential's account, not the run account, and cannot catch the mismatch.
intended_behavior: A rotation should re-key and revoke on exactly the account(s) the credential logs in as on each target. That is the resolution the renderer and the ProxyJump chain use: the host's SSH username, else the credential's username, and bastion.Username for a jump host. The verification test should authenticate as that same account. Then a successful group guarantees that normal runs work with the new key and that the old key is gone from the account it protected.

trace.description: An org admin (requireOrg with PermCredentialsWrite) starts the rotation. credentials.Rotate records PreviousPublicKey (rotate.go:89) and enqueues the group.
Enqueues one rotate_key per host or bastion target that references the credential, plus a dependent connection_test per host target, with a snapshot of the targets.
username := cred.Username. It falls back to the rendered or bastion username (host.Username) only when empty, and is shipped as both the login username and pulsix_user (the authorized_key user).
The rotation follow-up test replaces the rendered ansible_user with cred.Username, so the gate verifies K2 only on the credential's account.
If all succeeded, FinishRotation seals K2 onto the credential and enqueueRevocations queues revoke_key for the snapshot targets.
K1 is removed only for pulsix_user (the credential username, system_claim.go:186). The run account (the host SSH username or the bastion username) keeps K1.

evidence.description: Run login user: user := ssh.Username. Only if it is empty is CredentialUsers[credential] used, and the result becomes ansible_user.
ProxyJump hops dial bastion.Username@address:port.
On a bastion target, host.Username = bastion.Username, but rotateKindPayload and revokeKindPayload override it with cred.Username when that is set.
rotate_key login and pulsix_user use cred.Username first.
revoke_key login and pulsix_user use cred.Username first.
The rotation verification probe's username is overridden to cred.Username, replacing the rendered user set at queue_sql.go:887.
The worker logs in as payload.Username and passes the same value as pulsix_user to the playbook.
Installs the new public key for pulsix_user only.
Bootstrap also installs the key for cred.Username (or the default user). This is how K1 typically ends up on the credential's account while a host override points runs elsewhere.

conditions.description: An org admin starts the rotation as part of normal use. No attacker action is needed to create the gap. Whoever holds the old key K1 benefits, for example the party a leaked key reached.

A target whose run account differs from the credential's non-empty username: either a host with a host-level SSH username override, or a jump host whose username differs from its credential's username.
The old key K1 authenticates both the run account and the credential's account on that target. Otherwise rotate_key fails and nothing changes.

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of a leaked old key K1 whose rotation an org admin triggers. Equivalently, an admin who relies on rotation to retire K1.
payloads: render.Input{SSH: {web1: {Username: "deploy", CredentialID: cred}}, CredentialUsers: {cred: "ansible"}}; bastion jump-01 {Username: "jumper", CredentialID: cred}; credential {Kind: ssh_key, Username: "ansible"}; rotate_key, rotation connection_test and revoke_key claims built through SQLQueue.buildPayload with dummy keys
instructions: Copy the repository to scratch. Move the internal/jobs test files that need the DB harness out of the copy, because testcontainers is not in the offline module cache. Add internal/jobs/v05_rotation_account_test.go (package jobs) with minimal DB-free fakes for the box, renderer, credentials, bastions, templates and pins.
Render host web1 with the real render.Render, using host SSH username 'deploy' and a credential whose username is 'ansible'. Read ansible_user via connPortAndUser.

Build the rotate_key, rotation connection_test and revoke_key claims for web1, and the rotate_key and revoke_key claims for bastion jump-01 (username 'jumper'), through SQLQueue.buildPayload. Compare the usernames with the run account.
Run in the approved sandbox: go test -count=1 -v -run TestV05RotationAccount ./internal/jobs/ (network none, read-only, 2 CPU, 2 GiB, 300 s).
execution.observed_result: host web1: run ansible_user="deploy" | rotate username=ansible pulsix_user=ansible | verify probe user=ansible | revoke username=ansible pulsix_user=ansible; jump-01: hop dial=jumper@10.0.0.9:22 | rotate host.username=jumper username=ansible pulsix_user=ansible | revoke pulsix_user=ansible. PASS. The SSH effect on a real target was not run, because the sandbox has no ssh or ansible; it follows from the authorized_key tasks keyed on pulsix_user.

remediation.strategy: Resolve the rotation account the same way the renderer does. For a host target, use the rendered ansible_user (host SSH username, then credential username). For a bastion target, use bastion.Username. Fall back to cred.Username only when that is empty. Use this account for rotate_key, the rotation connection_test and revoke_key. When the credential's own username differs from that account, also remove the old key from the credential's account where that account exists, because bootstrap installs the key there. Regression test: a host with an SSH username override and a credential with a different username must produce rotate, test and revoke claims whose pulsix_user and login equal the rendered ansible_user. A bastion target must use bastion.Username.

likelihood.reason: It needs a target whose run account differs from the credential's non-empty username, with the old key also authorized on the credential's account. That is a specific but realistic configuration (a host SSH username override or a jump-host user after bootstrap). It needs no attacker action beyond already holding K1.

impact.reason: A rotation reported as successful leaves the retired key authenticating as the account Pulsix manages the host through, usually a sudo-capable account. That defeats revocation of a leaked key on that target. It also breaks later runs on that target. The breakage is visible, but the remaining K1 authorization is not reported.

confidence.reason: Every trace and evidence line was re-read at 4f9c710. The account divergence was independently reproduced in the approved sandbox with the real renderer and the real claim builders. The authorized_key semantics in the playbooks are explicit. Only the end-to-end SSH effect on a real host was not executed.

title: Host agent can still inject chat mentions and masked phishing links into alert notifications via check-result item names
description: The backlog 7.13 fix for the run-1 record internal/notify/render.go:alertItemsText:agent-item-unsanitized refuses control characters and U+2028/U+2029 at ingest (checks.breaksLine) and replaces them at render (notify.oneLine). Both the run-1 record and the fix's own comment (internal/checks/samples.go:197, 'would let a host forge alert rows or chat markup') name chat markup as the problem, but nothing neutralises same-line chat markup. A host agent (root on one enrolled host, holding that host's mTLS identity; a lower-trust principal than the org admins who read the alert channel) can report a check result whose item is, for example, '/var @everyone [Re-authenticate Pulsix](https://evil.example/login)' (at most MaxItemLen bytes, no control characters). recordCheckResults copies it verbatim into checks.Observation, withinContract accepts it, alerts.reconcile builds the alert subject from the tuple's item, the alert-route follower copies it into notify.AlertItem.Item, and alertItemsText places it verbatim into the {{ alerts.items }} text, which the code documents as the human-text field for Discord/n8n-shaped chat bodies. escapedText only JSON-string-escapes it ('<' becomes \u003c, which the receiver decodes back to '<'), and the template grammar offers no chat-safe filter (only '| json'). In a Discord or Slack webhook body this would appear as a mass mention and a masked link inside a trusted Pulsix alert. Source and the hunter's sandboxed tests show the markup reaches the rendered webhook body byte-for-byte; whether the receiving chat platform turns it into a live mention or link is a third-party fact outside the source.
claimed_root_cause: Agent-chosen check_key/item/metric are bounded only by length and by breaksLine/oneLine (control characters, U+2028/U+2029). Neither ingest (checks.withinContract) nor render (notify.alertItemsText/oneLine/escapedText) neutralises chat-markup metacharacters ('@' mentions, '<!...>' and '<url|text>', '[text](url)') or Unicode format/bidi characters before the value is placed into the alerts.items text that admin-authored chat webhook templates embed.

Batch handed to checks.Service.RecordObservations, the only ingest path for check results
Only length and breaksLine (control chars, U+2028/U+2029) are checked; '@', '<', '>', '[', ']', '(', ')' and Cf characters pass

Stored alert subject item copied unchanged into notify.AlertItem.Item for the routed batch
Item concatenated into the alert line after oneLine, which replaces only control/line-separator runes
alerts.items text form is alertItemsText; escapedText (line 133) only JSON-string-escapes it
Rendered body carrying the verbatim chat markup is posted to the admin-configured webhook endpoint

evidence.description: breaksLine refuses only unicode.IsControl, U+2028 and U+2029
The fix's own comment states the threat includes forging 'chat markup' in mails and webhook bodies, yet the check covers only line-breaking characters

The fix's regression test feeds 'ACTION REQUIRED @everyone' and asserts only the line count and absence of control characters, not that the mention is neutralised
Backlog 7.13 lists '@everyone' and phishing text as part of the problem but closes it with a line-break/control-character-only fix

blockers: Whether Discord/Slack/Teams (or the operator's chosen chat endpoint) render '@everyone', '<!channel>', '[text](url)' or '<url|text>' from a webhook body built with {{ alerts.items }} as a live mention or masked link is a third-party provider fact not observable from source or the offline sandbox

Whether a deployment routes alert batches to a chat webhook whose admin-authored template embeds {{ alerts.items }} without provider-side mention suppression (for example Discord allowed_mentions) is a deployment fact
Local evidence (agents/h04-notify-items/artifacts/evidence.txt, evidence2.txt) and source show only that the markup reaches the rendered body byte-for-byte; neither shows a rendered mention or link

validation_plan.local: In a scratch copy, run the DB-free tests TestH04AlertItemsCarryChatMarkup (internal/notify) and TestH04IngestAcceptsChatMarkupItem (internal/checks) under the approved Docker sandbox; both pass today, showing ingest accepts and render emits the markup verbatim inside {"content":"{{ alerts.items }}"}. After a fix (a chat-safe text form for alerts.items that defuses '@', '<', '>', '[', ']' and strips Cf bidi/format characters, and/or refusing those characters at ingest for item/check_key/metric), the same tests must fail on the verbatim-markup assertion while TestAlertItemsTextKeepsOneLinePerAlert keeps passing.

Delete the dummy org and webhook afterwards.

title: Outbound webhook policy blocks only AWS's IPv6 metadata address; other providers' IPv6 metadata endpoints in fc00::/7 are dialled
description: The webhook SSRF policy is meant to refuse cloud metadata addresses. The package contract says so at policy.go:6-7. It refuses link-local IPv4 (169.254.0.0/16) and lists four further metadata literals: 100.100.100.200, fd00:ec2::254, 192.0.0.192 and 168.63.129.16. The only IPv6 one is AWS's fd00:ec2::254. All other ULA space (fc00::/7) is allowed as private self-hosted space. None of the IPv4-in-IPv6 extractors (NAT64 well-known, IPv4-compatible, SIIT, 6to4, Teredo, ISATAP, operator NSPs) matches a ULA address. So the IPv6 metadata literals that other providers publish pass Policy.Check. Examples are Google Compute Engine's fd20:ce::254 and Oracle Cloud's fd00:c1::a9fe:a9fe; the OCI address carries 169.254.169.254 in its low 32 bits, under a prefix no extractor recognises. AWS's other ULA service address fd00:ec2::23 also passes. A sandboxed local run during this audit (audit artifact agents/v17-outbound/artifacts/evidence.txt, a scratch-only test against unmodified policy.go under golang:1.27.1-alpine with no network) confirmed that NewPolicy(nil, nil).Check returns nil for all three, while it refuses fd00:ec2::254 and 169.254.169.254. An org admin (channels.write) can store a webhook channel pointing at http://[fd20:ce::254]/... or http://[fd00:c1::a9fe:a9fe]/.... Any MFA-complete user can create an org and become its owner. Through Send test or an alert delivery, the admin can then make the manager send POST/PUT requests there. The literal is dialled directly and no proxy is used. The requests carry attacker-chosen headers (for example Metadata-Flavor: Google, or Authorization: Bearer Oracle) and an attacker-templated JSON body. send.go reads the response body into io.Discard, so the reach is a blind write plus a status-code and connect-error oracle, not credential disclosure. Whether the metadata service is reachable from the manager at all depends on the provider and on IPv6 networking. The shipped compose stack does not enable IPv6.
claimed_root_cause: blockedRanges() (internal/outbound/policy.go:31-55) implements metadata protection as a short list of literal addresses whose only IPv6 entry is AWS's fd00:ec2::254/128. That list mirrors the architecture spec's enumeration (2026-09-10-pulsix-architecture-design.md:727-728). fc00::/7 is otherwise allowed wholesale as self-hosted private space, and the embedded-IPv4 extractors (policy.go:73-138, nat64.go) do not match ULA addresses. A provider's ULA metadata endpoint therefore passes Policy.Check (policy.go:191-201) unrefused.

trace.description: An org admin (notifyChannelScope with tenancy.PermChannelsWrite, line 178) triggers a synchronous send to a webhook channel whose URL they stored via POST or PUT notification-channels (lines 115-116 and 140-141). Any MFA-complete session user can create an org (org_handlers.go:71-75) and become its owner.

Checks syntax only: scheme http/https, a non-empty host, no userinfo, no fragment. It therefore accepts http://[fd20:ce::254]/computeMetadata/v1/ or http://[fd00:c1::a9fe:a9fe]/opc/v2/. By design, the address check is deferred to dial time.

Builds a POST/PUT request to the stored URL with the operator's headers (lines 168-170; validate.go reservedHeader refuses only transport and X-Pulsix- names, so Metadata-Flavor and Authorization are accepted) and the templated body, then calls s.http.Do (line 181) on the shared outbound client.

The literal IPv6 host parses as a netip.Addr (line 85) and is passed to Policy.Check. When Check returns nil, it is dialled directly (lines 103-104). Proxy is nil and redirects are refused, so the dial goes nowhere else.

No blockedRanges entry contains fd20:ce::254 or fd00:c1::a9fe:a9fe; the only IPv6 metadata entry is fd00:ec2::254/128 at line 43. p.embedded (line 196) finds no IPv4 address in a ULA address, so Check returns nil and the connection to the metadata service goes ahead.

evidence.description: Package contract: cloud metadata addresses are refused unless PULSIX_NOTIFY_ALLOW_CIDRS lists them. Private ranges including fc00::/7 are allowed (lines 8-10).

The only IPv6 metadata entry is AWS's fd00:ec2::254/128, so ULA metadata endpoints are meant to be in scope. Lines 44-45 add provider-specific IPv4 literals for Oracle (legacy) and Azure, but no GCE or OCI IPv6 endpoint is listed.

embeddingPrefixes covers 64:ff9b::/96, ::/96, ::ffff:0:0:0/96, 2002::/16 and 2001::/32. isatapEmbeddedIPv4 (line 128) requires 0000:5efe or 0200:5efe in bytes 8-11. Neither matches fd00:c1::a9fe:a9fe, so the 169.254.169.254 it embeds is never checked.

The spec lists the refused set as loopback, link-local (169.254.169.254 included), unspecified, multicast, broadcast, 100.100.100.200 or fd00:ec2::254. The implementation matches the spec, and the spec itself omits the other providers' IPv6 metadata endpoints.

The response body is read into io.Discard. Only the status code or a URL-redacted transport error is recorded (lines 181-198), which limits the impact to a blind write plus an existence/status oracle.
fd00:ec2::254 is the only IPv6 metadata case in TestPolicyCheck; no GCE, OCI or other ULA metadata address is tested.

blockers: The IPv6 metadata endpoint addresses (GCE fd20:ce::254, OCI fd00:c1::a9fe:a9fe, AWS fd00:ec2::23) and the methods and paths they accept are provider facts, not repository facts. Examples are whether GCE answers POST at all and whether a guest-attributes PUT exists and is enabled. They need confirming against provider documentation pinned to the deployment date. No network access was allowed in this audit.

Reachability depends on the deployment. The manager must run on such a provider on an IPv6-enabled (dual-stack or IPv6-only) instance, with a network path from the manager process to the node's metadata endpoint. The shipped deploy/compose/docker-compose.yml has no enable_ipv6 or host networking, and nothing in the repository establishes such a deployment.

Source limits the impact to a blind POST/PUT plus a status and connect-error oracle, because send.go discards the response body. Whether any write-capable metadata path, or a service such as EKS Pod Identity at fd00:ec2::23, has a meaningful effect without a credential the attacker lacks is a provider fact.

validation_plan.local: Already done in the approved sandbox: a scratch-only test calling outbound.NewPolicy(nil, nil).Check showed nil for fd20:ce::254, fd00:c1::a9fe:a9fe and fd00:ec2::23, and ErrBlocked for fd00:ec2::254 and 169.254.169.254 (artifact evidence.txt). As a regression gate, add those three literals with allowed=false to the TestPolicyCheck table in internal/outbound/policy_test.go and run go test -count=1 -run 'TestPolicyCheck$' ./internal/outbound/ inside the same sandbox. The test fails today and must pass after the fix: /128 entries with reason 'cloud metadata' in blockedRanges. Check is pure and uses no network.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed, on a dedicated test VM only. Use a GCE or OCI instance with IPv6 enabled (dual-stack), running the manager in the shipped deployment shape: compose, plus a variant with host networking or IPv6 enabled if the owner supports one. With a dummy org and a dummy admin account, create a webhook channel to http://[fd20:ce::254]/computeMetadata/v1/ (GCE, header Metadata-Flavor: Google) or http://[fd00:c1::a9fe:a9fe]/opc/v2/instance/ (OCI, header Authorization: Bearer Oracle). Press Send test and record the delivery's last_error. An HTTP status such as 404, 405 or 200, instead of 'destination address is not allowed' or a connect error, shows the metadata service was reached. Use only these read-only root paths and never target a writable metadata path.

title: Unauthenticated POST /api/v1/setup/complete runs a 64 MiB argon2id hash on every call, even after setup is complete, with no rate or concurrency limit
description: The completion route for the first-run wizard stays registered and public for as long as the instance runs. setup.Service.Complete hashes the supplied admin password with argon2id (t=3, m=64 MiB, p=2) before it checks whether an instance administrator already exists. The route also has none of the per-address limiters that the other authentication routes use. On a completed instance, any anonymous client can send a small (~200 byte) well-formed JSON body. Each request is refused with 409, but only after the manager has allocated 64 MiB and spent roughly 120-260 ms of argon2id work on two threads. Live heap and CPU grow linearly with concurrent requests. Neither the HTTP server, the route nor the service bounds that concurrency, so a single client can degrade or exhaust the memory and CPU of the shared manager process. That process serves every organization's REST API, logins, the SPA and the gRPC worker/agent endpoint.
root_cause: Service.Complete calls auth.HashPassword (internal/setup/service.go:237) before the AdminExists gate inside InTx (service.go:243-250). registerSetupRoutes attaches only withAudit, not withAuthRateLimit, to the public route (internal/api/setup_handlers.go:107). Nothing bounds concurrent argon2id work across the process.
intended_behavior: Once setup is complete, the route must refuse cheaply, as Complete's own doc comment promises for a completion 'discovered before this call started' (service.go:226). A public route that can reach argon2id must also sit behind a per-address limit and a concurrency bound before it hashes.

trace.description: Public route on the root huma API (registered at internal/api/api.go:503). It needs no session or bearer token. Body validation checks only the shape: password minLength 12, email format, slug pattern.
Passes the anonymous body straight to deps.Setup.Complete.
in.validate() is the only check before hashing, and any well-formed body passes it.

auth.HashPassword runs argon2.IDKey with 64 MiB of memory, 3 passes and 2 threads (internal/auth/password.go:16-18,35). This happens before the InTx/AdminExists check at lines 243-250 returns ErrAlreadyCompleted, which the handler maps to 409 at setup_handlers.go:279-280.

evidence.description: hash, err := auth.HashPassword(in.AdminPassword) comes before s.store.InTx (line 243) and the tx.AdminExists check (lines 244-249). No AdminExists check runs before the hash.
argonMemory = 64 * 1024 KiB (64 MiB), with argonTime = 3 and argonThreads = 2. argon2.IDKey is called at line 35.
The route's only options are DefaultStatus and withAudit. withAuthRateLimit appears only at auth_handlers.go:106, mfa_handlers.go:178, passkey_handlers.go:218 and member_handlers.go:264.
The router-wide middleware is RequestID, Logger, Recoverer, securityHeaders, the session cookie and requireMFAForExplorer. None of them throttles requests or bounds concurrency.
The http.Server sets only ReadHeaderTimeout. Nothing caps connections or request concurrency in front of the handler.
The compose stack publishes manager port 8080 directly. The repository defines no container memory limit, no GOMEMLIMIT and no proxy rate-limit or in-flight middleware.

conditions.description: None. The route is public and needs no session, token or secret.

The attacker can reach the manager's HTTP listener, which the compose stack publishes on 8080, or reach it through the optional proxy. Any limits in a reverse proxy or gateway that the operator adds are outside the repository.
Applies to every instance for its whole lifetime. On a completed instance, every call is refused with 409 after the hash, so the only effect is resource consumption.

execution.attacker_perspective: An anonymous network client able to send HTTP POST requests to the manager.
payloads: POST /api/v1/setup/complete {"admin_email":"a@x.test","admin_password":"aaaaaaaaaaaa","admin_name":"A","org_slug":"a","org_name":"A"}

setup.Service.Complete(ctx, setup.Input{AdminEmail: "a@x.test", AdminPassword: "aaaaaaaaaaaa", AdminName: "A", OrgSlug: "a", OrgName: "A"}) against a store whose AdminExists returns true, 1 call and then 3 concurrent calls
instructions: Copied the repository into the verifier scratch directory. Removed store_sql_test.go from the copy only, because it needs testcontainers. Added internal/setup/audit_v07_test.go, which defines its own concurrency-safe completedStore: AdminExists always returns true, and the store counts AdminExists calls and writes. The test needs no database and does not reuse the hunter's harness.

The test measures runtime.MemStats.TotalAlloc and wall time for Status, which is the cheap baseline, and for Complete with the payload body: one call, then 3 concurrent goroutines. It asserts that every Complete returns ErrAlreadyCompleted, that each call allocates at least 60 MiB, and that the store sees zero writes.

Ran it in the approved Docker sandbox: no network, read-only root and source, cap-drop ALL, 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 512 pids, 300 s timeout. Command: go test -count=1 -v -run TestAuditV07CompleteOnCompletedInstance ./internal/setup/.

The sandbox run's output is the audit artifact agents/v07-availability/artifacts/evidence.txt (not a repository source). Its line 3 records Complete x1 allocating 67154904 bytes (64.0 MiB) in 120 ms, and its line 4 records x3 concurrent allocating 201417016 bytes (192.1 MiB, HeapSys 199.7 MiB). Every call returned ErrAlreadyCompleted with zero writes, and Status allocated 584 bytes.
execution.observed_result: Status: 584 bytes, ~18 us. Complete x1: 67154904 bytes (64.0 MiB) allocated, 120 ms, ErrAlreadyCompleted. Complete x3 concurrent: 201417016 bytes (192.1 MiB) allocated, HeapSys 199.7 MiB, 334 ms, all ErrAlreadyCompleted. AdminExists was called 5 times (1 Status + 4 Complete, each after its hash), with 0 writes. PASS. This matches the hunter's independent run: 64.0 MiB per call, and 256.1 MiB for 4 concurrent calls.

remediation.strategy: First, refuse a completed instance before hashing. Add a cheap s.store.AdminExists check before auth.HashPassword and keep the in-transaction re-check for the concurrent first-run race. Second, attach withAuthRateLimit to POST /api/v1/setup/complete; a refused 409 is a 4xx, so it keeps its slot. Third, as defence in depth for every route that reaches argon2id (login also runs a dummy hash for unknown e-mails), bound concurrent argon2id work. Use a semaphore of about runtime.NumCPU() slots that the password hasher owns and that is injected through the constructor, in line with the repository's no-package-state rule. Regression test: on a store whose AdminExists returns true, Complete returns ErrAlreadyCompleted without hashing. Assert this through TotalAlloc staying under 1 MiB or through a hasher seam.

code_changes.fixed_code: }, func(o *huma.Operation) { o.DefaultStatus = http.StatusCreated }, withAuthRateLimit(deps), withAudit("completeSetup", "setup"))

likelihood.reason: Needs no authentication, has no rate limit and takes a trivial well-formed JSON body. It is reachable on every instance for its whole lifetime, from a single source address.

impact.reason: Each ~200-byte request costs 64 MiB of allocation and about 0.1-0.25 s of argon2id work on two threads. Live heap and CPU grow linearly with concurrent requests and nothing bounds them, so a flood can degrade or OOM the single manager process that every organization shares. The effect is transient (restart: unless-stopped, and it recovers when the flood stops) and causes no loss of data, confidentiality or integrity. Operator-added memory limits or proxy limits outside the repository may reduce, but not remove, the degradation.

confidence.reason: The order in the source is unambiguous: the hash comes before the gate. No router, route or server bound exists in the repository. Two independent sandbox harnesses each measured 64 MiB per refused call, growing linearly with concurrent calls.

title: A managed host's returned facts can replace the pinned SSH options (and add a ProxyCommand) through pulsix_ssh_common_args
description: The worker enforces host-key pins (and the aliased jump chain) by moving each host's SSH common args into the inventory host var pulsix_ssh_common_args. It then forces the extra var ansible_ssh_common_args to the template "{{ pulsix_ssh_common_args | default('') }}". The extra var has the highest precedence, but the variable it reads is an ordinary inventory host var. In Ansible, host facts outrank inventory host vars. The run's ansible.cfg and subprocess env leave inject_facts_as_vars at its default of True, so any module result's ansible_facts become top-level host vars. ansible-core's clean_facts drops facts named like connection variables (ansible_ssh_*, ansible_connection, interpreter and become names), but it does not know the pulsix_ name. A managed host controls the JSON its modules return, because its own python runs them. A compromised managed host can therefore return ansible_facts {"pulsix_ssh_common_args": "-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ProxyCommand=<cmd>"}. A TOFU-accepted impostor of an unpinned host can do the same. That includes the setup module's output when a play gathers facts. On that host's next SSH connection in the same run, the forced template resolves to the attacker's value, the pinned StrictHostKeyChecking=yes/HostKeyAlias options disappear, and ssh runs the ProxyCommand on the worker as the ansible-playbook uid (the play uid in production). That uid can read and write the run's work dir through the group bits ShareWorkDir mirrors: keys/ with every run credential's key file, inventory.json, vault/ password files, extravars and the shared known_hosts. It can read the credentials the run uses for other hosts. It can also rewrite known_hosts to drop other hosts' pins for the rest of the run. This was reproduced with the worker image's ansible-core 2.21.4. A fact returned by a module replaced the pinned options on the next ssh command line, and the ProxyCommand created a marker file on the controller. With ANSIBLE_INJECT_FACT_VARS=False, or with the carrier renamed to an ansible_ssh_-prefixed name, the pins were kept and no command ran.
root_cause: The connection-security value moved from ansible_ssh_common_args, a name ansible-core itself strips from returned facts, into a pulsix_-prefixed host var that ansible-core does not protect. The forced extra var then reads it back through a template, and that template resolves facts above inventory host vars. Nothing turns off fact injection: there is no inject_facts_as_vars = False in ansibleCfgText and no ANSIBLE_INJECT_FACT_VARS in the subprocess env. The worker's reserved-name guard (inventory.go:279, ansiblevars.Forbidden) checks only the claim's extra vars. The design comment at inventory.go:356-361 counts only playbook authors as able to redefine the variable and overlooks module-returned facts from managed hosts.
intended_behavior: Pinned per-host SSH options (StrictHostKeyChecking=yes, HostKeyAlias=pulsix-host-<id>, the aliased ProxyJump chain) must hold for every connection of the run whatever a managed host returns. Only the worker, or by design a playbook author, may change them. A managed host must never be able to remove its own pin or inject ssh options that run commands on the worker.

trace.description: The worker starts ansible-runner/ansible-playbook against the claim's managed hosts. The JSON of every module result, including ansible_facts (and the setup module's facts when a play gathers them), comes from the managed host's python, which a compromised or impostor host controls. ansible-core merges these facts into that host's variables.

For a pinned host, the options '-o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes -o HostKeyAlias=pulsix-host-<id>' are prepended to its ansible_ssh_common_args (which also carries the aliased ProxyJump chain) and stored at line 484.

The value moves into the inventory host var pulsix_ssh_common_args, and ansible_ssh_common_args is deleted from the inventory (called at inventory.go:229). An inventory host var ranks below host facts.

The generated ansible.cfg sets host_key_checking, retry_files_enabled, local_tmp and ssh_args but not inject_facts_as_vars. The subprocess env (runner.go:481-486) does not set ANSIBLE_INJECT_FACT_VARS either. `ansible-config dump` with this cfg in the worker image reports INJECT_FACTS_AS_VARS(default) = True.

The forced extra var ansible_ssh_common_args = "{{ pulsix_ssh_common_args | default('') }}" is templated per task with the host's variables, facts included. A fact of that name replaces the pinned options on the ssh command line, and a ProxyCommand in it runs on the worker. This was observed with ansible-core 2.21.4.

evidence.description: pinnedCommonArgsVar = "pulsix_ssh_common_args" is the host var that carries the pinned options and the jump chain.
The design comment says that what stays possible is a playbook redefining pulsix_ssh_common_args (by design, spec §14). It does not consider facts returned by managed hosts.
The worker's reserved-name guard applies only to the claim's extra vars. Nothing checks module-returned facts.
The [defaults] section has host_key_checking = True but no inject_facts_as_vars = False.

The subprocess env adds ANSIBLE_HOST_KEY_CHECKING, ANSIBLE_RETRY_FILES_ENABLED, ANSIBLE_SSH_ARGS, ANSIBLE_CONFIG, ANSIBLE_LOCAL_TEMP and HOME, and nothing that disables fact injection. stripPrivateEnv (runner.go:805) removes any inherited ANSIBLE_* setting.

ShareWorkDir mirrors the owner bits onto the group so the play uid can read and write the run's files (keys/, inventory.json, vault/, env/extravars, known_hosts; names at layout.go:19-58). That is what a ProxyCommand running as the play uid can reach.
The pulsix_ prefix is forbidden only for user input (template/webhook extra vars, schema fields). Facts that managed hosts return are never checked.

conditions.description: The attacker controls a managed host targeted by a run, so it can control the JSON its modules (or the setup module) return. That could be a compromised host, or an impostor accepted by trust-on-first-use for an unpinned host. No Pulsix account is needed.

The run opens another SSH connection to that same host after the fact is returned, which is any multi-task play or any play with gather_facts. The single-task ad-hoc playbook (playbook.go:189-195, gather_facts false) offers no later connection.

Default inject_facts_as_vars=True, which the worker does not change (ansible-core 2.21.4 in the worker image; the default is deprecated for removal in 2.24). With PlayUID set, the ProxyCommand runs as the play uid with group access to the run's work dir. In the embedded worker it runs as the manager uid, which was not examined here.

execution.attacker_perspective: A compromised managed host (or a TOFU impostor of an unpinned host) in a Pulsix organization that answers a playbook run's module invocation with crafted ansible_facts.
payloads: {"changed": false, "ansible_facts": {"pulsix_ssh_common_args": "-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o ProxyCommand=\"touch /tmp/run/h12-marker\""}}
instructions: In the worker image (noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev, ansible-core 2.21.4) with no network, reproduce the worker's run layout with dummy data. Use an executable inventory script whose host 'victim' (127.0.0.1:2222) has pulsix_ssh_common_args='-o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes -o HostKeyAlias=pulsix-host-<uuid>'. Use an extra-vars file equal to forcedConnectionVars (ansible_ssh_common_args="{{ pulsix_ssh_common_args | default('') }}", ansible_ssh_args with -F ssh_config and the run's known_hosts). Use ansible.cfg as rendered by ansibleCfgText and the subprocess env from Runner.subprocessEnv.

Use a play with gather_facts false. T1 is ping over ssh (ignore_unreachable). T2 is a custom module that prints the payload JSON; it runs with connection: local to stand in for module output produced by the managed host's python, and is parsed and cleaned by the same action-plugin path. T3 debugs the resolved values. T4 is ping over ssh (ignore_unreachable). T5/T6 stat the marker locally.
Run ansible-playbook -vvvv -i inv.sh -e @extravars.json play.yml and compare the 'SSH: EXEC' lines of T1 and T4. Then check for /tmp/run/h12-marker.
Repeat with ANSIBLE_INJECT_FACT_VARS=False (control), and again with the carrier renamed to ansible_ssh_pulsix_common_args (fix check).
execution.observed_result: Audit artifacts of the validation run (agents/v08-ssh-pins/artifacts/evidence.txt, evidence2.txt, evidence3.txt; not repository sources) record the following. In the worker image, ansible-core 2.21.4 reports INJECT_FACTS_AS_VARS(default) = True with the run's ansible.cfg, and its clean_facts strips returned facts matching the magic variable names, the common connection vars, ^ansible_<connection>_, ansible_become_* and ^ansible_.*_interpreter$, so a pulsix_* fact is not matched. Playbooks that rely on top-level ansible_* facts would then need ansible_facts.*, and the ansible-core 2.24 default change will require that anyway. likelihood.reason: The attacker must already control a managed host targeted by a run (or impersonate an unpinned host at first contact). After that, exploitation is deterministic: any later SSH task to that host in the same run, which most playbooks have, especially with fact gathering on.

impact.reason: It crosses the managed-host to worker boundary. The host removes its own pin and runs arbitrary commands on the worker as the play uid. That uid can read every credential key file, the inventory document, vault password files and extra vars of the run, which means credentials for the other hosts in the run. title: Run-output redaction misses a secret shown double-escaped when a module result already holds it as JSON text
description: The worker removes a claim's secrets from ansible's display text by literal substring replacement over a fixed set of spellings: raw, Go-JSON-escaped and Python-JSON-escaped (backlog 7.9), plus base64 forms and private-key lines. A module result string can itself be JSON text, for example a debug of a to_json value, a command that prints a JSON config file, or an API response body. The secret then sits in that string already JSON-escaped once, and ansible-core's result display (Python json.dumps) escapes it a second time. If the secret contains a double quote, a backslash or a control character, this doubly escaped spelling is on no list, so the secret survives in the forwarded display text. The structured res copy of the same event is redacted, because the worker decodes it and the single-escaped spelling then matches. The display copy is not. Any org member with jobs.read (viewer and up) reads the display copy through the events list and the SSE stream. Decoding it twice gives back the exact secret. This was reproduced end to end with real ansible-runner 2.4.3 and ansible-core 2.21.4 from the worker image: both an ok debug task at default verbosity and a failed shell task leaked the secret.
root_cause: newRedactor (internal/worker/runner/redact.go:49-71) adds only one level of JSON escaping per secret through jsonSpellings (redact.go:106). redactor.text (redact.go:197) does a literal strings.ReplaceAll per listed spelling. A secret held JSON-escaped inside a result string, then escaped again by the result display, matches none of them. eventPayload redacts the decoded res structurally (redact.go:241), which removes the single-escaped form, but redacts the raw display string with text() (redact.go:246). The two copies of the same data therefore disagree.
intended_behavior: Every display spelling of a claim secret that ansible can produce for an event, including a result string that carries JSON text, is replaced by [redacted] before the event leaves the worker. Viewers with jobs.read must never see a credential, a secret extra var or a secret inventory var that a task printed (internal/jobs/redact.go:1-5).

trace.description: ansible-runner's --json event stream (task output under the control of the play, not the viewer) is consumed by streamEvents with newRedactor(job), built from the claim's Redact list and credentials.
Each secret gets its raw form plus jsonSpellings(v), one level of Go and Python JSON escaping. No second-level spelling is added.
Each mapped event (ok, failed, ...) is forwarded with red.eventPayload(ev).

The display text ('ok: [h] => {...}' or 'fatal: [h]: FAILED! => {...}') is redacted with text(). The res copy is decoded first and redacted per string (line 241), which catches the single-escaped form.
Literal strings.ReplaceAll per listed spelling. The double-escaped spelling Xk9\\\"q\\\\Lm2#vT matches none of them and is forwarded intact.
The manager takes the worker's payload as is.
The payload is stored in job_events unchanged (normalizePayload passes valid JSON through, events.go:500-506).
requireOrg(PermJobsRead) returns the stored payload (job_handlers.go:333) to any org member with jobs.read, which the viewer role holds (roles.go:113).

evidence.description: jsonSpellings returns only the single-level Go and Python JSON string bodies of v.
res is decoded and redacted per string, so the structured copy is cleaned while the display copy of the same data is not.
The repo pins ansible-core 2.21.4's display as Python json.dumps of the result, the producer of the second escaping level.
States the boundary: viewers with jobs.read see run logs and must never see a credential, secret extra var or secret inventory var a task printed.
jobs.read is granted from the viewer role up.
normalizePayload stores valid JSON payloads unchanged. No manager-side redaction pass exists.

conditions.description: The secret (credential password or token, secret extra var or secret inventory var) is at least 4 characters and contains a double quote, a backslash or a control character. A private key's long base64 lines stay covered by line-by-line redaction.

A task's displayed result holds text that already carries the secret JSON-escaped, and ansible shows that result. Examples: a debug of a to_json value (shown at default verbosity), a failed command or shell task whose stdout is a JSON document, or a JSON response body.
The reader is an org member or token with jobs.read (viewer) who is not otherwise entitled to the secret. The task output is produced by an operator-written playbook. The viewer cannot trigger it.

execution.attacker_perspective: An org viewer reads a run's event log through GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}/jobs/{id}/events or the SSE stream, after an operator's playbook showed a JSON document that contains a secret.
payloads: claim Redact entry (dummy secret): Xk9"q\Lm2#vT
playbook task 1: debug: msg="{{ {'db_password': secret} | to_json }}"
playbook task 2: shell: printf '%s' "$CFG"; exit 1 with environment CFG="{{ {'db_password': secret} | to_json }}" and ignore_errors: true
