Keep the runner_on_ok and runner_on_failed JSON lines (artifact evidence2.txt).

Copy the repository into scratch, put those two lines in internal/worker/runner/testdata/v09/events.jsonl and add a test that runs each line through ParseEvent, then newRedactor(&workerpb.Job{Redact: [secret]}).eventPayload, then decodes the forwarded display JSON and the inner JSON string.

Go sandbox (golang:1.27.1-alpine, no network, read-only, uid 65532, cap-drop ALL, 2 CPU, 2 GiB): go test -count=1 -v -run 'TestAuditV09RealAnsibleNestedJSON|TestRedactsPythonJSONSpelling' ./internal/worker/runner/ (artifact evidence.txt).
execution.observed_result: ansible-core 2.21.4 printed the debug result as ok: [localhost] => {"msg": "{\"db_password\": \"Xk9\\\"q\\\\Lm2#vT\"}"} at default verbosity, and the failed shell result's stdout and stdout_lines fields the same way. After the worker's real ParseEvent and eventPayload, both events' forwarded res reads {"db_password": "[redacted]"}. Both forwarded display stdouts still hold the spelling Xk9\\\"q\\\\Lm2#vT, which is not in the redactor's list. Decoding the display JSON and then the inner JSON string returns db_password equal to the exact secret. The existing TestRedactsPythonJSONSpelling still passes. Artifacts: agents/v09-job-output/artifacts/evidence.txt and agents/v09-job-output/artifacts/evidence2.txt. The manager-side storage and the API read are confirmed from source only, because they are DB-backed.

remediation.strategy: In newRedactor, also add a second JSON escaping level: every jsonSpellings form of every jsonSpellings form (Go and Python, four combinations). This covers a JSON document shown inside a result display. Add a regression test that uses the real ansible-core 2.21.4 display lines for a to_json debug and a failed command whose stdout is JSON, with a secret holding a quote and a backslash. Optionally (hardening), cover deeper nesting by iterating the escaping until it stops changing up to a small bound, or redact the decoded display JSON as well as the raw text.

likelihood.reason: Three things must coincide: a secret that contains a quote, a backslash or a control character; an operator-written task whose displayed result embeds that secret inside JSON text; and a result that ansible displays (any debug task, any failure, or verbose mode). The viewer cannot cause any of them.

impact.reason: A viewer-role member or a viewer token reads a credential password or token, a secret extra var or a secret inventory var verbatim. That crosses the viewer-to-secret boundary the redact list exists to enforce, within one org. It does not cross tenants.

confidence.reason: The miss was reproduced with real ansible-runner 2.4.3 and ansible-core 2.21.4 output from the worker image, fed through the worker's own ParseEvent and redactor in the sandbox. The double-escaped spelling is absent from the redact list, while the res copy of the same event is redacted. The storage and API pass-through is DB-backed and verified from source only: there is no manager-side redaction, normalizePayload passes JSON through unchanged, and the route is requireOrg(PermJobsRead).

title: A leftover play process can kill the between-jobs sweep, which runs as the same play uid and fails open
description: Backlog 7.21 added a sweep so that no play-uid process outlives its job. At loop start and after every job, the worker runs its own binary in sweep mode through the setuid helper as the play uid, and that process calls kill(-1, SIGKILL). The sweep therefore runs as exactly the uid it is meant to clear. After the helper's setuid(), its real, effective and saved uid are all the play uid. From then until kill(-1) runs, any play-uid process may SIGKILL it: during the rest of the helper, its execv, the Go runtime start-up of the worker binary and the argument dispatch. sweepPlayUID only logs the failure and the claim loop goes on to the next job. Take an operator whose play detaches a process and kills its own supervisor, the scenario the repository's own e2e test models. That operator can add a watcher that SIGKILLs every process carrying the sweep argument. The process then stays alive across all later jobs on that worker until the container restarts, including after the operator's membership or role is revoked. Every later job's work dir is opened 2770 to the play group, with run files mirrored to group rw. The leftover runs with that gid and can learn each new work dir's path from the later play's /proc/<pid>/cmdline, because ansible-runner is started as 'run <workdir>'. It can then read later jobs' revealed SSH keys and vault or become passwords, and rewrite their playbook, inventory or ansible.cfg before ansible reads them. That includes jobs launched by others: scheduled and webhook runs, and admin-run bootstrap and rotate_key jobs. For example, it can capture the new key from a rotation an admin runs after revoking the operator. The work-dir half of 7.21 still holds: run files are written while the dir is owner-only, so this does not bring back the run-1 symlink attack on worker-uid writes. Impact stays inside the organisation that owns the worker.
root_cause: sweepPlayUID (internal/worker/workdir.go:57-75) relies on a process running as the play uid to remove play-uid processes: setuid helper (setuid-exec.c:217), then execv of the worker binary (setuid-exec.c:254), then cmd/worker/main.go:69, then supervisor.Sweep's kill(-1) at sweep.go:30. Under Linux kill(2) rules, any other process of that uid can SIGKILL it before it acts. The failure is fail-open. It is only logged (workdir.go:71-74), and runOne's deferred cleanup (loop.go:319-322) and the Run claim loop (loop.go:185-234) carry on. Nothing checks afterwards, from a uid the play cannot signal, that no play-uid process remains.
intended_behavior: Once a job ends, no process of the play uid may survive into the next job (supervisor/sweep.go:10-17, workdir.go:45-51). If the worker cannot establish that, it must not claim another job.

trace.description: An operator's run job (jobs.run / playbooks.write) has its work dir opened to the play group, and its play is spawned as the play uid through the helper (args at runner.go:191, newRunnerCmd at 376). A localhost task detaches a process and SIGKILLs its play supervisor (same uid), so the process outlives the job.
When the job ends, the deferred cleanup calls sweepPlayUID (line 320) and then removeWorkDir.
Runs <helper> <play uid> <worker binary> __pulsix-play-sweep.

setuid(play_uid) from euid 0 sets the real, effective and saved uid to the play uid (read back at line 223). From here on, any play-uid process may signal this process. Observed: the leftover killed the helper itself at this stage in 6 of 10 rounds.
execv of the worker binary. The process then goes through Go runtime start-up as a play-uid process whose /proc/<pid>/cmdline names the sweep argument.
Dispatches to supervisor.Sweep only after runtime and package initialisation.
kill(-1, SIGKILL) would remove the leftover, but the leftover has already SIGKILLed this process.
CombinedOutput returns 'signal: killed'. The error is only logged, the loop claims the next job, and the leftover keeps play-uid and play-group access to every later shared work dir and play process.

evidence.description: sweepPlayUID has no return value. On failure it logs 'could not stop the play uid's leftover processes' (lines 71-74), and nothing stops the next claim.
The design comment notes that the play can kill its supervisor because both run as the same uid. The sweep repeats that pattern, since it also runs as that uid.

The read-back guarantees uid == euid == play uid before execv, and setuid() from euid 0 also sets the saved uid. That is exactly the condition under which kill(2) from another play-uid process is permitted. The worker-image run shows /proc status 'Uid: 65533 65533 65533 65533' for the swept helper.
Run calls runOne and goes back to ClaimJob whatever the sweep's outcome. The loop-start sweep at line 176 is fail-open in the same way.

Every later job's work dir root is chmodded with group bits mirrored from the owner plus setgid (2770), with files mirrored to group rw, for the play group. A surviving leftover has that gid, because the helper sets gid to worker_gid.
ansible-runner is started as 'run <WorkDir> ...'. The data dir is 0710 (loop.go:441), so the leftover cannot list it, but it reads the random work-dir path from the later play's /proc/<pid>/cmdline.
The image e2e test checks only a passive detached sleep, not a leftover that resists the sweep.

conditions.description: Operator or higher in the organisation (jobs.run / playbooks.write) to run a localhost task on that org's worker once. The leftover then persists after the role is revoked.

Playbook uid separation enabled (PULSIX_WORKER_PLAY_UID set, compose default 65533) on a Linux worker with the play supervisor. That is the configuration in which the sweep runs. The process namespace must be shared, as in the shipped image: no per-play PID namespace or cgroup exists in the source.

The leftover must SIGKILL the sweep between the helper's setuid() and the Go sweep's kill(-1). A /proc polling loop (Go in the golang sandbox, Python in the worker image) won 10/10 rounds in both independent runs.

execution.attacker_perspective: A process of the play uid that outlived its job polls /proc and SIGKILLs any process whose cmdline contains __pulsix-play-sweep.
payloads: Leftover loop: for pid in /proc: if b'__pulsix-play-sweep' in /proc/pid/cmdline: kill(pid, SIGKILL)
Production-shaped sweep invocation: /usr/local/bin/pulsix-setuid-exec 65533 /pulsix-worker __pulsix-play-sweep (the argv workdir.go:69 builds)
Single-uid helper stand-in for the HEAD-binary run: #!/bin/sh\nshift\nexec "$@"
instructions: Run A (HEAD worker binary, real Loop.sweepPlayUID): copy the source to scratch and add internal/worker/v10_sweep_evasion_test.go (the hunter's harness with renamed tests). In the approved golang sandbox (network none, read-only, uid 65532, cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, 2 CPU/2 GiB/512 pids, 300 s), run go test -count=1 -v -run 'TestV10' ./internal/worker/. The test builds ./cmd/worker, starts the leftover, and calls the production sweepPlayUID 10 times with PlayUID=65533 and a stand-in helper that only execs its argv.

Run B (real setuid-root helper, real uid separation): in noixdev/pulsix-worker:dev, with the worker-image variant flags (network none, read-only, limits, image USER 65532, ro mount of the scripts in evidence3.txt), run the control /usr/local/bin/pulsix-setuid-exec 65533 /pulsix-worker __pulsix-play-sweep without a leftover. Then start the leftover with pulsix-setuid-exec 65533 /usr/local/bin/python3 -I killer.py, and run the same sweep invocation 10 times, recording exit codes and the leftover's state.
execution.observed_result: Run A (evidence.txt): in 10/10 rounds sweepPlayUID logged level=ERROR "could not stop the play uid's leftover processes; a play may still be running" err="signal: killed" and returned normally in 1-2 ms. The leftover stayed alive (state S/R). PASS. Run B (evidence2.txt): the leftover ran with Uid 65533 65533 65533 65533. The control sweep invocation exited 2: the image binary predates sweep mode and falls through to config loading, so it was not killed by anything else. With the leftover present, all 10 sweep invocations exited 137 (SIGKILL), and the leftover stayed alive (state R). The leftover's kill(2) succeeded against the setuid helper itself after its drop (argv0 pulsix-setuid-exec, uids all 65533) in 6 rounds and against /pulsix-worker in 4. So the window opens at setuid-exec.c:217, before any Go code runs.

remediation.strategy: Fail closed, and do not let the swept uid run the sweep's critical section. (1) Treat a sweep that did not exit 0 as fatal: stop claiming jobs, or exit the worker so that a container restart clears every process. (2) After the sweep, have the worker check from its own uid that no process with real or effective uid == PlayUID remains, by scanning /proc/<pid>/status Uid:. If any remains, retry and then fail closed. (3) Remove the window: run each play in its own cgroup and use cgroup.kill, or a PID namespace whose init the worker controls, both of which the play cannot interrupt. Doing kill(-1) inside the static helper right after the drop only narrows the window, because Run B shows the helper is killable once setuid() returns. (4) Add a uidboundary e2e case where the leftover SIGKILLs processes carrying the sweep argument.

likelihood.reason: It needs a malicious operator-or-higher member of the same organisation who runs a localhost task, and the uid-separation feature turned on. The race itself is trivial and won every round in both local runs.

impact.reason: It defeats the 7.21 process guarantee completely. The operator's code persists on the org's worker across all later jobs and after their role is revoked. It can read later jobs' revealed credentials, including keys from rotations an admin runs to evict them, and rewrite their run files before ansible reads them. While the operator holds the role, reading job credentials is accepted by design (spec §14), so the delta is persistence past revocation and tampering with others' jobs. It stays within one organisation and does not reach the worker's certificate or key.

confidence.reason: Every trace line was checked against source at 4f9c710. Two independent local runs agree. Run A used the HEAD worker binary and the production sweepPlayUID, with only the uid change stubbed. Run B used the image's real setuid-root helper with real uid 65532 to 65533 separation and the production argv, and showed the swept process killable from the moment setuid() returns. The one gap is that the image's worker binary predates sweep mode. This does not affect the result, because 6 of 10 kills landed in the helper before execv.

title: A worker revocation that lands mid-call does not stop ClaimJob from handing the revoked worker a job payload
description: ClaimJob authenticates the worker once, in the gRPC interceptor (Server.authenticate -> lookupWorker -> workers.Service.GetBySerial), and then heartbeats, claims and ships a job without consulting the registry again. If an admin's revocation commits between that lookup and the claim UPDATE, the call still succeeds. The revoked worker receives a fully built job payload, which can include revealed inventory secrets, credentials, vault identities or SSH key material depending on the job kind, along with a registered binding token. buildPayload runs after the claim transaction commits and the handler returns its result unconditionally. So the payload ships whether the claim commits before or after Revoke's RequeueWorkerJobs. A claim that commits after RequeueWorkerJobs also leaves the job 'running' under the revoked worker until the reaper notices it. That includes a job the requeue just put back, which the in-flight call can re-claim. No layer on the path checks the worker's status: TouchWorkerByID updates by id with no status predicate, and while the revoke transaction holds the workers row lock it only blocks the call and then lets it continue. The ClaimJob SQL filters only on job status, org, zone and dependency. The project closed this exact race for RunEvents with a second lookupWorker after tracking (events.go:59-65), and backlog 2.57 states that a revoked worker cannot claim a new job. ClaimJob has no equivalent guard. A worker that keeps several ClaimJob calls in flight gets at most one job per call that passed the interceptor before the revocation committed.
root_cause: Authorization for ClaimJob is evaluated once, in the interceptor, and is not bound to the claim's state change. Neither the handler (internal/grpcsrv/claim.go) nor the claim transaction (internal/jobs/queue_sql.go SQLQueue.claim issuing jobs.sql ClaimJob) checks or locks the claiming worker's registry row, so a revocation committing in between is never observed.
intended_behavior: Revocation 'refuses every certificate of the worker from now on' (internal/workers/revoke.go Revoke; spec 2026-09-18 section 4), and backlog 2.57 records that a revoked worker can neither claim a new job nor report a result. No job may be claimed for, or a payload shipped to, a worker whose revocation has committed. A claim must either serialize before the revocation, so that RequeueWorkerJobs takes it back, or be refused.

trace.description: The gRPC interceptor handles a worker-certificate ClaimJob call (mTLS peer, CA-verified identity, method kind checked) and resolves the worker through lookupWorker, once, before the handler runs.
Workers.GetBySerial reads the registry row. At this instant the worker and certificate are not revoked (service.go:230), so the call is authorized and the row is stashed in the context.

Admin revocation commits RevokeWorker and RevokeWorkerCertificates in one write transaction (store_sql.go:246-262), then runs CloseWorker and RequeueWorkerJobs. Nothing here reaches an in-flight ClaimJob call.
Touch (TouchWorkerByID, UPDATE workers ... WHERE id) has no status predicate. While the revoke transaction is open it blocks on the row lock, and after the commit it succeeds.
Claims.Claim is called with a scope taken from the stale interceptor row. No registry re-check happens before or after it.
gen ClaimJob (jobs.sql:103-117) takes the oldest queued job of the org and zone and records worker_id as the revoked worker. The statement never consults workers.status.
After the commit, buildPayload reveals the job's credential and inventory material into the payload under the job's org scope, and a stream binding token is registered.
The payload and its binding token are returned to the worker whose revocation has already committed.

evidence.description: Sibling handler RunEvents re-runs lookupWorker after tracking the stream, because a revocation can commit after the interceptor's lookup (comment at lines 59-62). ClaimJob has no such guard.
The ClaimJob UPDATE filters on job status, org_id, zone_id and depends_on only. It has no join, predicate or lock on the claiming worker's row.
TouchWorkerByID updates by id with no status predicate, so the heartbeat succeeds for a revoked worker after RevokeWorker (workers.sql:65) releases its row lock.
RequeueWorkerJobs runs once, after the revoke commit. A claim that commits after it stays assigned to the revoked worker, and a payload built after any claim commit is shipped either way.
ClaimJob takes the worker only from the interceptor's context value. There is no later lookup.
GetBySerial is the only place worker or certificate revocation is enforced on the gRPC path, and ClaimJob reaches it only through the interceptor.
Backlog 2.57 states that a revoked worker can neither claim a new job nor report a result, and it relies on the interceptor alone for that. It does not consider a revocation landing during the call.

conditions.description: The caller holds a valid worker certificate (for example a compromised zone worker) that an org admin is revoking at that moment.

A ClaimJob call must pass the interceptor lookup before the revocation commits and reach the claim UPDATE after it. Keeping several calls in flight widens this window, and Touch blocking on the revoke transaction's row lock lines calls up behind the commit.
At least one queued job must exist in the worker's own org and zone at that moment, including jobs RequeueWorkerJobs just put back. Each in-flight call yields at most one job.

execution.attacker_perspective: A worker whose certificate is being revoked keeps ClaimJob calls in flight. Calls that the interceptor authorized before the revocation committed still claim and receive job payloads after it.
payloads: internal/grpcsrv/zz_verify_claim_revoke_test.go (scratch copy only): newHarness; h.issue("dummy-worker", orgID, zoneID, true); enqueueClaim(jobA), enqueueClaim(jobB); h.store.revokeAfterLookup = serial; client.ClaimJob(Version "0.0.0-test"); inspect h.store.revoked[serial] and h.srv.registry.lookup(jobA); a second client.ClaimJob
instructions: Copy the repository into the verifier scratch directory and add the test above to internal/grpcsrv. It uses the package's own fake worker store fixture revokeAfterLookup. The fixture lets the interceptor's lookup succeed and marks the serial revoked immediately afterwards, which is the same race fixture TestRevocationBetweenAuthAndTrackEndsTheStream uses for RunEvents.

Inside the approved Docker sandbox (golang:1.27.1-alpine, --network none, --read-only, --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, uid 65532, 2 CPU / 2 GiB / 512 pids, timeout 300 s, read-only source and module cache), run: go test -count=1 -v -run 'TestVerifyClaimAfterRevocation|TestRevocationBetweenAuthAndTrackEndsTheStream' ./internal/grpcsrv/
execution.observed_result: TestRevocationBetweenAuthAndTrackEndsTheStream passed: RunEvents refuses after the same race. TestVerifyClaimAfterRevocation logged 'in-flight ClaimJob: err=<nil> job_id="01a1985d-..." token_set=true', then 'registry after call: certificate revoked=true', then 'binding registered for claimed job: true', and the next ClaimJob returned code=Unauthenticated. The handler shipped a job and its binding token to a worker whose revocation had taken effect before the claim ran. The real-Postgres interleaving (Touch blocking on the RevokeWorker row lock and the absence of any status predicate) was established from source only, because DB-backed tests cannot run in this sandbox.

remediation.strategy: Bind the claim to the worker's current registry state inside the claim transaction. For a worker claim (workerID valid), first run a locking read of the worker row, SELECT 1 FROM workers WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'active' FOR SHARE, and claim nothing if it returns no row. Optionally also require an unrevoked worker_certificates row for the presented serial. Under READ COMMITTED this serializes with RevokeWorker's row update. A claim that waits on an open revocation re-reads the committed 'revoked' row and claims nothing. A claim that locks first commits before RevokeWorker can proceed, so RequeueWorkerJobs (which runs after the revoke commit) takes the job back. As defence in depth, mirror RunEvents: after Claims.Claim returns a job, re-run lookupWorker. On refusal, hand the job back through a new Claimer release port that requeues it bound to this worker id, drop the registry binding, and return Unauthenticated instead of the payload. Regression tests: the revokeAfterLookup fixture on ClaimJob must yield Unauthenticated with no job and no registry binding, and a store integration test must show that ClaimFor for a revoked worker returns nil.

code_changes.fixed_code:
-- name: LockActiveWorker :one
-- Claim-time check: shares the row lock RevokeWorker's UPDATE takes, so a
-- claim either commits before the revocation or sees it.
SELECT id FROM workers WHERE id = sqlc.arg(id) AND status = 'active' FOR SHARE;

likelihood.reason: This requires a worker certificate under active revocation, a queued job in its own zone, and a ClaimJob call that straddles the revocation commit. The window is short. A malicious worker can widen it by keeping many calls in flight, and Touch blocking on the revoke row lock helps.

impact.reason: The revoked worker receives the payload, possibly including revealed credentials, of at most one queued job per in-flight call. The jobs come from its own org and zone, right after revocation, and the same worker could have claimed them moments earlier. It is a non-atomic cut of an intended revocation guarantee, not a cross-tenant or cross-zone leak. The stray 'running' assignment is later recovered by the reaper.

confidence.reason: The verifier reproduced the result independently in the approved sandbox. The test used the package's own revocation-race fixture, the one the project uses to pin the equivalent RunEvents fix, and ClaimJob returned a job and binding token to a serial the registry already refused. Source shows that no layer re-checks worker status: there is no handler re-lookup, TouchWorkerByID has no predicate, and the ClaimJob SQL has no worker join. The real-Postgres timing was not executed, because DB-backed tests are forbidden here. It does not affect whether the gap exists, only how wide the window is.

title: Pending invitations outlive the inviting admin's removal, demotion or deactivation and cannot be revoked, so a removed admin can regain admin access
description: An org admin (members.manage) can create invitations of up to the admin role for any address, including one they control. On an instance without outbound mail the API returns the accept link to the inviter (member_handlers.go:154); with mail it goes to the inviter-chosen mailbox. Invitations stay valid for 7 days (InviteTTL). AcceptInvite and the PeekInvite/TakeInvite SQL check only the token hash, accepted_at and expiry. Nothing checks whether the issuer (invited_by) is still a member, still holds members.manage, or is still an active account. RemoveMember, ChangeRole (demotion) and DeactivateUser leave the issuer's pending invitations untouched. The API has no route to list or revoke pending invitations; the only invite DELETE is internal cleanup after a failed mail send. The SPA comment documents the missing list route. An admin who expects removal can mint admin invitations for alternate addresses in advance. After the owner removes or demotes them, or an instance admin deactivates them, they redeem a link anonymously and rejoin the organization as admin under a fresh account. The new admin account can mint further invitations before it is noticed. The owner therefore cannot fully evict a malicious admin through the product: invitation creation is audited, but outstanding invitations cannot be cancelled.
root_cause: The invite credential is not bound to its issuer's continuing authority and has no revocation path. tenancy.Service.AcceptInvite (internal/tenancy/service.go:410-463) adds inv.Role (line 459) on the strength of the token alone. PeekInvite and TakeInvite (internal/db/queries/tenancy_users.sql:69-70, 80-82) filter only on token_hash, accepted_at and expires_at. invited_by (00007_invites.sql:9) is written at creation and never read again. RemoveMember (service.go:542), ChangeRole (service.go:513) and DeactivateUser (service.go:571) never touch invites. The only invite routes are POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/invites and POST /api/v1/invites/accept.
intended_behavior: Removing, demoting or deactivating a member should end every authority that member delegated through pending invitations. At acceptance the issuer must still be an active member whose role holds members.manage, or the issuer's pending invites must be deleted as soon as they lose that authority. Org admins and owners should be able to list and revoke pending invitations.

trace.description: An admin passes requireOrg(PermMembersManage) and creates an invitation with role up to admin (owner is refused at service.go:332) for an address of their choosing.

When the mailer returns mail.ErrNotConfigured, the plaintext accept link is set on the result, and the handler returns it as accept_url (member_handlers.go:154). With mail configured it goes to the inviter-chosen address. The row stores invited_by (service.go:347), which no later code reads.

The owner removes or demotes the admin, or an instance admin deactivates them. Only the membership row is deleted or updated, or the user is disabled and their sessions and tokens revoked. Pending invites from this issuer stay valid.

Public route with no principal. The removed admin redeems the link anonymously with a new name and password. For an address with no account, checkAcceptor (service.go:469-482) requires only a name and an 8-character password.
Accepts any unaccepted, unexpired token hash. It has no condition on invited_by, org_memberships or users.disabled_at.
After creating the new account (service.go:437-441), adds the membership with inv.Role (admin) to the organization that removed the issuer.

evidence.description: TakeInvite: UPDATE invites SET accepted_at ... WHERE token_hash = $1 AND accepted_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now RETURNING *. PeekInvite (line 69) has the same filter. Neither has an issuer-authority condition.
invited_by uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) is stored. No trigger or query consults it at acceptance, on membership removal, or on demotion.

RemoveMember calls only GetMembership and DeleteMembership. ChangeRole (513) calls only UpdateMembershipRole. DeactivateUser (571) only disables the user and revokes sessions and API tokens. None touches invites.
AcceptInvite grants inv.Role from the token without re-validating the issuer.
The only invite DELETE is used by Service.Invite (service.go:377) to remove an invitation whose mail delivery failed. No route or service method revokes a pending invitation.
States that the API has no GET route listing pending invitations (only POST /invites and POST /invites/accept), so the Invitations tab is omitted. An owner cannot see or revoke them.
Returns inv.AcceptURL to the inviter. On an instance without outbound mail, that is the redeemable link.

conditions.description: Before losing authority, the attacker held the admin role (members.manage) in the organization and created one or more invitations.
The attacker redeems the invitation within InviteTTL (7 days) of creating it, after being removed, demoted or deactivated.
The attacker controls the invitation link: either the instance has no outbound mail (the link is returned in the API response), or the invited address is a mailbox the attacker controls.

execution.attacker_perspective: A malicious or about-to-be-removed organization admin who wants to keep admin access after the owner removes or demotes them, or after an instance admin deactivates their account.
payloads: svc.Invite(ctx, org.ID, admin, "admin-alt@example.test", tenancy.RoleAdmin) with a mailer returning mail.ErrNotConfigured; then either svc.RemoveMember(ctx, org.ID, RoleOwner, owner, admin) + svc.DeactivateUser(ctx, true, admin), or svc.ChangeRole(ctx, org.ID, RoleOwner, owner, admin, RoleViewer); then svc.AcceptInvite(ctx, uuid.Nil, inv.Token, "Alt", "long-enough-password")
instructions: Copied the repository to the verifier scratch directory. Added internal/tenancy/v12_invite_revoke_test.go (TestV12InviteOutlivesIssuerAuthority), which uses the package's existing in-memory fakeStore and fakeMailer with dummy principals. The fake's PeekInvite and TakeInvite mirror the real SQL filters. In the scratch copy only, store_sql_test.go was moved aside because it imports the testcontainers-backed testdb.

Ran `go test -count=1 -v -run 'TestV12InviteOutlivesIssuerAuthority|TestAcceptInvite' ./internal/tenancy/` in the approved Docker sandbox: no network, read-only root, source and module cache, uid 65532, cap-drop ALL, 2 CPU, 2 GiB, 512 pids, 300 s timeout.

Subtest removed_and_deactivated: the owner creates an org, a dummy admin is added, and the admin invites admin-alt@example.test as admin and receives the link. The owner removes the admin and an instance admin deactivates them. The link is then redeemed anonymously. Subtest demoted_to_viewer: same setup, but the owner demotes the admin to viewer before redemption.
Source check for the real store: TakeInvite and PeekInvite SQL, the RemoveMember, ChangeRole and DeactivateUser service paths, and the API route set contain no issuer check and no invite revocation.
execution.observed_result: removed_and_deactivated: issuer membership_err=not a member, disabled=true, pending invites=1. RESULT accept_err=<nil>, org_match=true, new_account=true, new_member_role=admin. demoted_to_viewer: issuer role=viewer, pending invites=1. RESULT accept_err=<nil>, org_match=true, new_account=true, new_member_role=admin. The existing TestAcceptInvite* tests passed (agents/v12-invite/artifacts/evidence.txt).

remediation.strategy: Bind invite validity to the issuer's live authority, and add revocation. (1) In PeekInvite and TakeInvite, require the issuer to still be an active member of the invite's org with a role that holds members.manage (owner or admin). The accept path runs without pulsix.org_id, so the RLS bypass policy lets the EXISTS subquery see org_memberships. (2) Delete the issuer's pending invites for that org in RemoveMember and in ChangeRole when the new role drops below admin. Delete all of a user's pending invites in DeactivateUser. Do this in the same transaction as the membership change where possible. (3) Add admin-only GET /orgs/{org}/invites and DELETE /orgs/{org}/invites/{id} routes, audited, so owners can see and revoke pending invitations, and surface them in the members page. Regression tests: an invite whose issuer was removed, demoted below admin, or deactivated before acceptance returns ErrNotFound and adds no membership; a revoked invite returns ErrNotFound.

code_changes.fixed_code:
-- name: TakeInvite :one
UPDATE invites AS i SET accepted_at = sqlc.arg(now)::timestamptz
WHERE i.token_hash = $1 AND i.accepted_at IS NULL AND i.expires_at > sqlc.arg(now)::timestamptz
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM org_memberships m JOIN users u ON u.id = m.user_id
              WHERE m.org_id = i.org_id AND m.user_id = i.invited_by
                AND m.role IN ('owner','admin') AND u.disabled_at IS NULL)
RETURNING i.*;

-- (apply the same EXISTS condition to PeekInvite)

-- name: DeletePendingInvitesByIssuerInOrg :exec
DELETE FROM invites WHERE org_id = $1 AND invited_by = $2 AND accepted_at IS NULL;

-- name: DeletePendingInvitesByIssuer :exec
DELETE FROM invites WHERE invited_by = $1 AND accepted_at IS NULL;

likelihood.reason: Requires an insider who already held admin and planned ahead by minting invitations before losing authority, then redeemed one within 7 days. There is no external attacker path.

impact.reason: The attacker regains the org admin role after the owner explicitly revoked it: credential writes and rotation, members, tokens, channels, alert routes and workers. Admin also grants operator-level job execution on the org's workers. The owner cannot list or cancel pending invitations, so the regained admin can mint new invitations faster than they are removed. A full eviction then needs database access or deleting the organization. The member list and audit feed show the new member after the fact.

confidence.reason: Independently reproduced at service level in the approved sandbox for both removal plus deactivation and demotion, using the package's own fake store, whose invite lookup mirrors the real SQL filters. The real store's PeekInvite and TakeInvite SQL, the RemoveMember, ChangeRole and DeactivateUser paths, and the complete invite route set were read and contain no issuer check or revocation. No migration trigger touches invites. The DB-backed path itself was not executed, because testcontainers is forbidden here.
